sections.title: Binding a Name to a Value
sections.body:
A **variable** is a name bound to a value, and `=` is the binding operator rather than the equals sign of mathematics: it means store the value on the right under the name on the left.

Declare with `const` when the name will never point at anything else, and with `let` when it genuinely must be reassigned. JavaScript evaluates the right-hand side first and only then rebinds, which is why `score = score + 10` reads sensibly instead of circularly.

`console.log()` prints its arguments on one line with a single space between them. Reassigning a `const` does not fail quietly - it throws a `TypeError` the moment that line runs.

annotations.text: score is let because line 6 rebinds it. Had this said const, line 6 would throw.
The right side is computed from the old value (42 + 10), then 52 is bound back to the same name.
Rebinding a const throws TypeError. The try/catch is here only so the example can print the error's name instead of stopping.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `withBonus(score)` which returns `score` plus a bonus of 10. `withBonus(42)` must return `52`.
checkpoint.explain: BONUS is a const because nothing in the function ever rebinds it, and naming it at all turns a bare 10 into something a later reader can understand. Returning the total rather than logging it is what lets a caller use the number, which is the difference between a function and a printout.
checkpoint.hint1: The bonus is already declared for you.
checkpoint.hint2: You need the `return` keyword, not console.log.

sections.title: Why const Is the Default and var Is Not
sections.body:
`const` is the default because a name that can never be rebound is one less thing to hold in your head while reading the rest of the file. Reach for `let` only at the moment you know a name must change, and treat that keyword as a signal to the next reader.

`var` is the older keyword and it is **function-scoped**: a `var` written inside a block is the very same variable as the one outside it, so its value leaks out. It is also **hoisted**, meaning the name already exists holding `undefined` on lines above its own declaration.

`let` and `const` are block-scoped and stay inside the nearest pair of braces, which is why modern JavaScript does not reach for `var` at all.

annotations.text: This is not a new variable. It is the same total from line 1, so the 99 escapes the if-block.
This IS a new variable, alive only between the braces. The outer count still holds 1.
early is hoisted, so the name already exists here holding undefined. Written with let, this line would throw a ReferenceError instead.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill in the two keywords so this prints `70`, choosing the most restrictive keyword that still works for each name.
checkpoint.explain: MAX_HP is never rebound, so const both documents that fact and enforces it. hp is rebound on the third line, so it has to be let - and the moment you are forced to write let, you have told the reader exactly which of the two names they need to keep watching.
checkpoint.hint: Only one of the two names is ever assigned a second time.

sections.title: The Primitive Types and typeof
sections.body:
Every value has a **type**. JavaScript has seven primitive types - `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `bigint` and `symbol` - and the first five carry everything on this floor.

There is only one number type, so `7` and `7.0` are the same value and `7 / 2` is `3.5` rather than `3`. `undefined` is what a declared-but-unassigned name holds, while `null` is a value you assign on purpose to mean **nothing here**.

`typeof x` reports the type as a lowercase string, and it carries one famous wart: `typeof null` is `"object"`, a bug from 1995 that can no longer be fixed without breaking the web.

annotations.text: A comparison evaluates to a boolean, so ready holds true - you rarely write true by hand.
Declared with no value. unset holds undefined, which is a real value, not an error.
typeof null is "object", which is wrong and always has been. Learn it as a fact about the language, not a rule you can reason out.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print? Write all four lines.
checkpoint.explain: A pair of quotes is the entire difference between the first two lines, and it changes what every later operator will do with the value. The last line is the language's oldest wart: null is a primitive, yet typeof reports "object" for it.

sections.title: Joining Text, Templates, and Conversion
sections.body:
`+` does two different jobs. Given two numbers it adds; given a string on either side it **concatenates**, converting the other operand to text first - which is why `"5" + 1` is `"51"` while `"5" - 1` is `4`, since only `+` has a string meaning and every other arithmetic operator coerces to number instead.

A **template literal** is written between backticks and evaluates whatever expression you place inside `${ }`, so the fixed text and the computed values stay in one readable piece rather than being sewn together with `+`.

`Number(x)` and `String(x)` convert deliberately. Convert at the boundary where text arrives, and no later line has to wonder what it is holding.

annotations.text: Same output as line 4 with none of the quote-and-plus bookkeeping. Backticks, not quotes.
raw is text, so + joins and prints 255. Nothing is raised - this is the bug that looks like an answer.
Converting first makes + mean addition again, giving 30.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints exactly `total: 10`.
checkpoint.explain: Without the conversion the expression would be "8" + 2, and + would join rather than add, printing total: 82. Inside a template literal you may place any expression, so the arithmetic happens before the surrounding text is assembled.
checkpoint.hint: One blank converts text to a number, the other is the operator that then adds.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
guided-practice.explain: Each line rebinds the same name using whatever it holds at that instant, so the program has to be read top to bottom rather than solved as a set of equations. If these were equations, `gold = gold * 4` would have no solution at all.
guided-practice.hint: Work out the right-hand side first, then write down gold's new value.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all four lines.
guided-practice.explain: JavaScript has one number type, so there is no separate integer division to fall back on and `7 / 2` keeps the half. `%` is what is left after that division and `**` raises to a power - both stay inside the same single number type, which is why line 2 reports it twice.
guided-practice.hint: Two values in one console.log land on one line, separated by a space.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write both lines.
guided-practice.explain: The two inner lines look identical and behave completely differently: `var a` reuses the outer binding, so 5 escapes the braces, while `let b` creates a second binding that dies at the closing brace. That leak is the whole reason `var` was replaced rather than merely discouraged.
guided-practice.hint: Only one of the two keywords respects the braces.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all four lines.
guided-practice.explain: As soon as one side of `+` is a string the whole operation becomes concatenation, and the result stays a string as evaluation runs left to right - which is how `2 + "3" + 4` reaches "234" rather than 9. `-` has no string meaning at all, so it converts "10" to a number and subtracts.
guided-practice.hint: Evaluate + strictly left to right, asking at each step whether either side is text.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these lines into a program that turns a wage typed as text into a day's pay and reports it.
guided-practice.explain: Every line consumes the name the line above it created, so the data dependencies fix the order completely - no other arrangement even runs. Converting immediately after reading means the two lines below never have to think about text again.
guided-practice.hint: Find the only line that uses no earlier name; that one goes first.

guided-practice.prompt: Give the value of `total` after each of the last three lines runs.
guided-practice.explain: Only one value exists at a time and each line replaces it, so the order of the lines is the entire meaning of the program. `%` gives what is left after dividing: 30 is four sevens with 2 to spare.
guided-practice.hint: Carry the number from one line into the next; 30 divided by 7 leaves a remainder.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `greet(name)` which returns a greeting built with a **template literal**. `greet("Mira")` must return the string `Hello, Mira!`.
guided-practice.explain: A template literal keeps the sentence intact and readable, whereas the `+` version splits one human phrase across three fragments and two operators. The empty-name case still returns a well-formed string because substitution never inspects what it is pasting in.
guided-practice.hint1: Template literals use backticks, not quotes.

guided-practice.prompt: This should return the next level up, but it throws `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable`. Fix it. `nextLevel(1)` must return `2`.
guided-practice.explain: The error is not about the arithmetic but about the promise the declaration made: `const` says this name is bound once, and the next line breaks that promise. The honest fix is `let` where the name really does change - or dropping the intermediate name and returning `level + 1`, which needs no rebinding at all.
guided-practice.hint1: Read the error literally: something is being assigned to a constant.
guided-practice.hint2: Which line rebinds a name that was declared const?
guided-practice.hint3: Change const to let - or return level + 1 and delete the extra name.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `describe(value)` which returns the value's type and the value itself, separated by a colon and a space. `describe(42)` must return `number: 42`, and `describe(null)` must return `object: null`.
guided-practice.explain: `typeof` already hands back a string, so it drops straight into a placeholder with no conversion of its own, and the second placeholder converts the value to text for you. The null case is the one to remember: the value prints as null while its reported type is "object".
guided-practice.hint1: typeof value is an expression, so it can go inside ${ }.
guided-practice.hint2: Two placeholders in one template literal, with ": " between them.

exam.prompt: A program runs `let x;` and then `console.log(typeof x);`. What is printed?
exam.explain: A `let` declaration with no initialiser still binds the name; it simply binds it to the value `undefined`, and `typeof` reports that as the string "undefined". A ReferenceError would mean the name does not exist at all, which is a different failure with a different fix.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write all four lines.
exam.answer:
Level 7 Mira
Level 7 Mira
Next: 8
Next: 71
exam.explain: The first two lines agree, so the template literal is purely a readability win - until the last line, where `+` has already turned the expression into concatenation before the 1 arrives. A placeholder evaluates its whole expression first, which is exactly what protects `${level + 1}`.
exam.hint: On the last line, ask what type the left-hand side has by the time the 1 is reached.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so the first console.log prints `30` and the second prints `255`.
exam.explain: The same `+` produces 30 on one line and 255 on the next, and nothing but the types decided which. Converting explicitly states your intent in the code, so a reader never has to work out which meaning of `+` is in play.
exam.hint: Both blanks are conversion functions, and they pull in opposite directions.

exam.prompt: Which of these expressions produce a value whose `typeof` is `"string"`?
exam.explain: Explicit conversion, concatenation and template substitution all end in text, while plain arithmetic and `Number()` stay numeric. Every one of these expressions looks numeric on the page, which is precisely why the type has to be reasoned about rather than eyeballed.

exam.prompt: Order these fragments into a working function `tagOf(value)` that returns, for example, `42 is a number`.
exam.explain: `kind` must be bound before the line that reads it, and nothing can sit after the closing brace and still belong to the function. Naming the type before using it costs one line and makes the returned sentence readable at a glance.
exam.hint: A name has to exist before the line that uses it, and the brace closes the body.

exam.prompt: `"5" + 1` evaluates to `"51"`, but `"5" - 1` evaluates to `4`. Explain why the same left-hand value behaves so differently, and say what you would write instead to make the first expression produce `6`.
exam.explain: `+` is the only arithmetic operator with a second, string meaning, so it joins the moment either side is text, while `-` has no such meaning and therefore converts to a number first. Nothing throws, which is what makes this dangerous - the fix is to convert at the boundary with `Number("5") + 1` rather than to distrust the arithmetic.
exam.hint: Ask which of the two operators has a meaning for text at all.

exam.prompt: Trace `value` through this program. Write text values in double quotes and numbers bare, exactly as you would type the literal.
exam.explain: One name carries a different type at different moments, so `+` joins on the second line while `%` does arithmetic two lines later. Tracking the type beside the value - not just the digits - is what tells you which meaning of an operator is about to apply.
exam.hint1: Line 2 is string work, not addition.
exam.hint2: Number("66") is the moment the type changes.
exam.hint3: 66 % 10 is the remainder after dividing by ten.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
exam.explain: `message` survives the block because `var` is scoped to the function rather than the braces, so a name you meant to keep private is visible to everything below. `hidden` genuinely no longer exists after the closing brace, and `typeof` is the one operator that can ask about a missing name without throwing a ReferenceError.
exam.hint: One of the two inner names outlives the closing brace.

exam.prompt: `rawScore` arrives as text from a form. `addBonus("40")` should return the number `50`, but it returns the string `"4010"`. Fix it.
exam.explain: Nothing threw, which is why this class of bug reaches production: `+` saw a string and did exactly what it promises for strings. Converting at the point the text enters the function repairs every line below it at once, whereas patching the result afterwards leaves the same trap for the next line you add.
exam.hint1: The arithmetic is fine; look at the type of what came in.
exam.hint2: What does + do when one side is a string?

exam.prompt: Write `receipt(item, rawPrice, quantity, rawPostage)` for a shop. `rawPrice` and `rawPostage` arrive as text; `quantity` is already a number. The total is the price times the quantity, plus the postage. Return a single string of the form `3 x potion = 17 coins`, so `receipt("potion", "5", 3, "2")` returns exactly `3 x potion = 17 coins`.
exam.explain: Skip the conversion on the postage and `15 + "2"` quietly becomes "152" - the multiplication would have coerced for you, but `+` never does, so the operator that looks safest is the one that bites. Every name here is const because nothing is ever rebound, and the zero cases need no special handling: multiplying by zero and pasting the result into the template falls out of the same code.
exam.hint1: Convert both text values before doing any arithmetic with them.
exam.hint2: The order matters: price times quantity first, then add the postage.

sections.title: The Fork in the Path
sections.body:
An `if` statement runs the block in its curly braces only when the condition in the round brackets is true. Adding `else if` offers alternatives, and a closing `else` catches everything left over.

JavaScript tests the conditions **top to bottom and stops at the first true one**, so every branch below the winner is skipped however true it might be. That makes the order of the branches part of the logic rather than a matter of taste.

Because a block is ordinary code, an `if` can sit inside another one. The braces alone decide what belongs to what - indentation is for human eyes only, and JavaScript ignores it completely.

annotations.text: 31 > 30 is true, so this branch runs and the two below it are never even tested.
Skipped. It would also have been true, but the chain already found its answer.
This else belongs to the inner if, so it means over 30 but not over 40.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: Exactly one branch of a chain can ever run. The third condition is also true for 7, but JavaScript stopped looking the moment the second one matched, so the order of the branches decided the answer.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Equal
sections.body:
JavaScript ships two equality operators and they are not interchangeable. `===` is **strict**: it answers true only when the two operands have the same type **and** the same value. `==` is **loose**: when the types differ it quietly converts one side before comparing, which is why `1 == "1"` is true while `1 === "1"` is false.

`!==` and `!=` are their negations and inherit exactly the same behaviour. Reach for `===` and `!==` by default, because a comparison that changes your data before answering is a comparison you cannot predict at a glance.

annotations.text: Same digit, different types - strict equality refuses it.
Loose equality turns the string into the number 1 first, so this one is true.
The empty string is converted to 0 before the comparison, and 0 == 0 is true.
null and undefined are loosely equal to each other, but strictly equal to nothing at all.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: A string of digits read from a form or an input field is still a string. The strict pair reports the type mismatch honestly; the loose pair converts it away, which is how a value that is not a number ends up counting as one.

sections.title: Truthy, Falsy and the Ternary
sections.body:
Any value at all can be used as a condition, not only a boolean. JavaScript has exactly **eight falsy** values - `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` - and treats absolutely everything else as **truthy**, including `"0"`, `"false"` and `-1`.

The **ternary** operator is an if/else squeezed into an expression: `condition ? valueWhenTrue : valueWhenFalse`. It produces a value instead of running statements, so it fits where an `if` cannot - in the middle of an assignment, or as the thing a function hands back.

annotations.text: Zero, empty and absent: the four falsy values you will meet every day.
Both of these strings hold characters, so both are truthy however false they read.
The ternary hands back one of two values, which is why it can sit to the right of an =.
0 is falsy, so an empty shelf reports itself without a single comparison being written.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so `stockLabel` returns "in stock" when `count` holds a non-zero number and "sold out" when it is 0.
checkpoint.explain: The question mark opens the choice and the colon separates the two results, so the whole line is one expression that `return` can carry. Handing `count` straight to the ternary leans on falsiness, which is why no comparison with 0 is needed.

sections.title: The Switch and Its Fall-Through
sections.body:
A `switch` compares one value against a list of cases using `===`, the same strict rule as before - so `switch ("2")` never matches `case 2`. Execution jumps to the first matching case and then **keeps running downwards until it meets a `break` or a `return`**. That is called fall-through.

Fall-through is a default, not an accident, and it is the pitfall of the statement: forget a `break` and the cases beneath yours run too. Stacking labels with nothing between them uses it deliberately, letting several values share one body, and `default` catches whatever matched nothing.

annotations.text: A case with no body falls into the next one, so child and student share a single result.
Execution starts here, then falls into case 3 because no break stopped it.
This break is why [four] never joins the string.
The string "2" is not strictly equal to the number 2, so default runs.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `sound(animal)` returning `"meow"` for `"cat"`, `"woof"` for `"dog"` and `"???"` for anything else. Use a `switch`.
checkpoint.explain: Returning from inside a case leaves the whole function, so it ends the switch as firmly as `break` does and no fall-through is possible. `default` is what turns an unknown animal into a defined answer instead of `undefined`.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: Zero is not greater than zero, so both tests fail and the chain lands on `else`. A boundary like this is where a stray `>=` would quietly change the meaning of the whole function.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: The last four lines compare the same two values and disagree twice, purely because of which operator was chosen. `!==` and `!=` are not different questions - they are the exact negations of `===` and `==`, and they inherit the conversion or the refusal along with it.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so `speedLabel(kph)` returns exactly one label: "too fast" above 120, "cruising" above 50, and "slow" otherwise.
guided-practice.explain: Chaining with `else if` is what makes the branches mutually exclusive. Three separate `if` statements would each be tested on their own, and 130 would match the first two rather than only the one you meant.

guided-practice.prompt: You are pricing a used vehicle. Write `resellPrice(originalPrice, age)` returning 80% of the original price when the vehicle is less than 3 years old, 50% when it is more than 10 years old, and 70% for everything in between. Return the number itself.
guided-practice.explain: The two boundary ages are the whole exercise: 3 is not less than 3 and 10 is not more than 10, so both fall through to the middle band. Ordering the branches so the last one needs no condition of its own is safer than writing `age >= 3 && age <= 10` and getting one of the two signs wrong.
guided-practice.hint: Two conditions and a final fallback are enough - the in-between band needs no test of its own.

guided-practice.prompt: `isZero(value)` should answer whether `value` is the number zero. It currently answers `true` for the empty string and for `false` as well. Fix it so only the number `0` passes.
guided-practice.explain: Loose equality converts the other operand to a number before comparing, and `""`, `false` and `"0"` all convert to 0 - so the test was really asking "does this become zero", not "is this zero". One extra `=` narrows the question back to the one that was intended.
guided-practice.hint: The condition is already the answer; the only problem is which equality operator asks it.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: Falsiness is about the value being empty, zero or absent - never about what the value looks like. A single space and the string `"0"` both contain a character, so both count as true in a condition, which is exactly why a blank-looking form field can still sail through an `if (field)` check.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `parity(n)` returning the string `"even"` when `n` divides by two exactly and `"odd"` when it does not. Use the ternary operator rather than an `if` statement.
guided-practice.explain: A ternary is an expression, so it can be returned directly and the whole function collapses to one line. The negative case is the one worth checking: `-3 % 2` is `-1` in JavaScript rather than `1`, so comparing the remainder against `0` is safe while comparing it against `1` would not be.
guided-practice.hint: condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse - and the condition here is a remainder test.

guided-practice.prompt: A form hands you its two number fields as strings. Write `addAsNumbers(a, b)` returning the **numeric** sum, so `addAsNumbers("5", "3")` is `8` and not `"53"`. It must still work when the arguments are already numbers.
guided-practice.explain: `+` is the one arithmetic operator with two jobs: given a string on either side it joins rather than adds, while `-`, `*` and `/` have no string meaning and convert to numbers on their own. Converting explicitly with `Number()` states the intention in the code instead of leaving it to the operator to guess.
guided-practice.hint: Number("5") is 5, and Number(5) is still 5 - so converting twice is harmless.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these fragments in the order that defines `fee(kind)`, returning 0 for a child and 12 for everyone else.
guided-practice.explain: A `switch` needs its own braces inside the function braces, and every `case` label ends with a colon rather than opening a block of its own. `default` goes last because it is the catch-all, and the two closing braces unwind in the reverse of the order they were opened.

guided-practice.prompt: Li Mei tells customers how long a drink will take. Write `timeToMixJuice(juice)` returning `0.5` for `"Pure Strawberry Joy"`, `1.5` for `"Energizer"` and for `"Green Garden"`, `3` for `"Tropical Island"`, `5` for `"All or Nothing"`, and `2.5` for anything else. Use a `switch`.
guided-practice.explain: Two drinks with the same answer become two stacked labels above one body - fall-through used on purpose, rather than the same `return` copied twice. The empty string is not on the menu and is not special-cased either, so it lands in `default` like any other unknown order.
guided-practice.hint: A case with no body of its own falls straight into the next case.

exam.prompt: `"7" == 7` is `true` but `"7" === 7` is `false`. Which sentence explains the difference?
choices: `==` compares the characters, while `===` compares where the values are stored in memory.
`==` converts one operand so the types match and then compares; `===` refuses to convert and demands the same type as well as the same value.
`===` compares three things - the type, the value and the variable name - so it needs a variable on both sides.
`==` is an older spelling of `===` kept for compatibility, and the two always agree.
exam.explain: Loose equality runs a conversion step first, so it answers a question about what the values could become rather than about what they are. Strict equality has no such step, which is what makes its answer predictable without knowing the conversion rules by heart.

exam.prompt: Which of these values are **falsy** - that is, `Boolean(value)` is `false`?
exam.explain: Only the empty, zero and absent values are falsy. A string is judged on whether it holds characters, never on what those characters spell, so `"0"` and a lone space are both truthy - and `-1` is a perfectly ordinary non-zero number.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: `+` means "join" the moment either side is a string, while `-` and `*` have no string meaning and convert to numbers instead - which is why one operator turns 5 and 3 into 53 and the next turns them into 2. The last line reads left to right: 2 + 2 is 4 while both sides are numbers, and only then does the string arrive and turn the result into "42".

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: Matching a case is an entry point, not a boundary: execution begins at `case 3` and then keeps going downwards through `case 4` because nothing stopped it. The `break` inside case 4 is what saves case 5, and case 2 is untouched because fall-through only ever runs forwards.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `stockLabel(count)` returns "in stock" whenever `count` is a non-zero number and "sold out" when it is 0. Judge `count` by its own truthiness - do not compare it with anything.
exam.explain: A bare value in the condition slot is converted to a boolean for you, so `count` alone already asks "is there any stock". The colon is what separates the two results of the ternary; without it the expression is incomplete and the file will not even parse.

exam.prompt: `x` holds the one-character string `"0"`. Give the value of each expression below - each one is `true` or `false`.
exam.code: const x = "0";
exam.explain: This value is truthy in an `if` and yet loosely equal to `false`, because the two mechanisms convert differently: a condition asks whether the string is empty, while `==` turns both sides into numbers first and gets 0 == 0. Strict equality is the only line here that reports what `x` actually is.

exam.prompt: Write `waterState(celsius)` returning `"solid"` at 0 degrees or below, `"gas"` at 100 or above, and `"liquid"` anywhere in between.
exam.explain: Both boundaries belong to the extremes, which is the whole difference between `<` and `<=` here, and getting either one wrong shows up only at exactly 0 or exactly 100. Handling the extremes first lets the final `return` need no condition at all, because everything that reaches it has already been ruled out twice.
exam.hint: Once the first two returns have run, nothing is left to test.

exam.prompt: The two amounts arrive from a form, so they are strings. `totalPrice("100", "5")` should be `105` but returns `"1005"` instead. Fix it so the function always returns a number.
exam.explain: Nothing is broken about the `+`: it saw a string and did what `+` does to strings, which is join them. This bug is invisible in testing whenever the inputs happen to already be numbers, so the fix is to convert at the boundary where untrusted text enters rather than to hope about what the caller sends.
exam.hint: The operator is fine. The types reaching it are not.

exam.prompt: Days are numbered with 0 for Sunday through to 6 for Saturday. Write `dayType(dayNumber)` returning `"weekend"` for 0 and 6, `"weekday"` for 1 to 5, and `"unknown"` for any other number. Use a `switch` with stacked labels rather than a chain of `if`s.
exam.explain: A switch matches discrete values, so a range has to be spelled out label by label - seven labels for two answers, which is exactly when an `if` on `>=` and `<=` would have read better. `default` is doing real work here: without it, 7 and -1 would fall out of the switch and the function would return `undefined`.
exam.hint: The two weekend days are not adjacent, so they need their own pair of stacked labels.

exam.prompt: Write `displayName(name)` returning `name` itself when it holds something, and `"anonymous"` when it does not. Decide with the truthiness of the value itself and a ternary - do not compare against `""`.
exam.explain: Testing truthiness catches the empty string and a missing argument with one condition, where `name === ""` would let `undefined` straight through. It also decides the two awkward cases for you: `"0"` and a lone space hold characters, so they are names and are returned unchanged.
exam.hint: A missing argument is undefined, and undefined is falsy - so one condition covers both empty cases.

exam.prompt: A logger uses `switch (level)` with `case "warn":` and `case "error":`, each logging its own message, and no `break` anywhere. Called with `"warn"` it logged both messages. Explain what the missing keyword changes, and why stacking two `case` labels with nothing between them is not the same mistake.
exam.explain: A matching case says where to start, not where to stop, so without `break` or `return` execution keeps running through every case beneath it. Stacked labels exploit the same rule deliberately: there is no body to run in between, so several values arrive at one shared body rather than accumulating several bodies.

lesson.title: Naming the Work, and the Scopes That Hold It

sections.title: Two Ways to Make a Function
sections.body:
A **function declaration** starts with the `function` keyword followed by a name, as in `function double(n) { ... }`. A **function expression** is the same machinery used as a value: you write it on the right of an `=` and store it in a `const`, usually with no name of its own.

The difference that bites is **hoisting**. A declaration is lifted to the top of its scope before any line runs, so you may call it above where it is written; a function expression only comes into existence when its own line is reached.

`return` hands a value back to the caller and ends the call there. A body that finishes without one hands back `undefined` - not an error, just a value that will fail somewhere else, later, far from the function that produced it.

annotations.text: Legal: the declaration below is hoisted, name and body together, before anything runs.
A function expression. Moving this call above line 7 would throw - const bindings are not hoisted usably.
Calling is the same either way: the name, then parentheses holding the arguments.
shout prints HI and then falls off the end, so the outer log receives undefined.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Both functions compute the same 5, but only one gives it back. logSum displays it and returns nothing, so `captured` holds undefined - the value that makes a program fail three functions away from the mistake.

sections.title: Arrows and the Implicit Return
sections.body:
An **arrow function** is a shorter way to write a function expression: the parameter list, then `=>`, then the body. With exactly one parameter the parentheses around it are optional, and with no parameters at all you write an empty pair `()`.

When the body is a single expression there is an **implicit return** - the value of that expression is handed to the caller with no `return` keyword anywhere in sight.

The moment you wrap the body in braces you are writing statements again, and a statement body returns `undefined` unless you write `return` yourself. That single rule accounts for most arrow-function bugs.

annotations.text: Concise body: the expression n * n is the return value, no keyword needed.
One parameter, so the parentheses may be dropped. Zero or two or more parameters always need them.
Braces open a statement body, so this one has to say return explicitly.
Braces with no return: the multiplication happens and the result is thrown away.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `4 2`.
checkpoint.explain: The arrow always sits between the parameter list and the body, but what the body owes you changes with its shape: a bare expression is returned for you, a braced block is not.

sections.title: Parameters, Arguments and Defaults
sections.body:
**Parameters** are the names in the definition; **arguments** are the values at the call. JavaScript never checks that the two lists are the same length - a parameter with no matching argument is simply `undefined`, and an extra argument is quietly ignored.

A **default parameter** is written with `=` in the parameter list, as in `function greet(name, greeting = "Hello")`. It fires on exactly one condition: the argument is `undefined`. Passing `0`, `""` or `null` is passing a real value, so the default stays out of the way.

Defaults are evaluated left to right when the call happens, which is why a later default is allowed to mention an earlier parameter.

annotations.text: Two parameters, but nothing forces a caller to supply both.
greeting takes the value "Hello" only when the caller leaves it out.
A default may refer to a parameter to its left, because defaults resolve left to right.
Passing undefined explicitly is indistinguishable from passing nothing - the default still fires.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `preparationTime(layers, avgTime)` returning `layers.length * avgTime`, the minutes needed to prepare a lasagna. When `avgTime` is not supplied, assume `2`. So `preparationTime(['sauce', 'noodles'])` returns `4`.
checkpoint.explain: The default belongs in the parameter list, not in the body: writing it there means the fallback is part of the function's signature and is visible to anyone reading the first line.

sections.title: Scope, and the Function That Remembers
sections.body:
A pair of braces makes a **block**, and a name declared with `let` or `const` lives only inside the block that declared it. The older `var` ignores blocks entirely: it is scoped to the whole enclosing **function**, so a `var` written inside an `if` is still there after the `if` has finished.

An inner function can read the names of the function that encloses it, and that link survives even after the outer function has returned. A function that keeps an outer variable alive this way is a **closure**.

Every call to a factory like `makeCounter` builds a fresh set of local names, so two counters made by the same factory never share a number.

annotations.text: blockOnly exists between these braces and nowhere else.
functionWide survives the block, because var is scoped to the function, not the braces.
This inner function is returned; it keeps count alive after makeCounter has finished.
A second factory call builds a second count, so this prints 1 rather than 3.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: `a` and `b` are two different functions built from the same body, and each closed over the `n` created by its own call to makeTicket. Closures capture a binding, not a value shared across the program.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Both functions build the same string; only one hands it back. The third line appears because showTag reaches the end of its body without a return, and a JavaScript function that does so evaluates to undefined.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a function declaration `totalTime(layerCount, minutesInOven)` returning the total cooking time in minutes: two minutes of preparation per layer, plus the minutes already spent in the oven. `totalTime(3, 20)` returns `26`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
function totalTime(layerCount, minutesInOven) {

}
guided-practice.hint: Two minutes per layer is a multiplication, and the oven time is added on top.
guided-practice.explain: A declaration binds the name for the whole enclosing scope, so the order of definitions in the file stops mattering. Without the `return` the arithmetic still runs and is then discarded, which is why a forgotten return shows up as undefined rather than as an error.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so both arrow functions work and the program prints `42 -5`.
guided-practice.explain: The fat arrow separates the parameter list from the body in every arrow function. What differs is the body: a bare expression is returned automatically, while braces make it a statement list that returns nothing until you say so.

guided-practice.prompt: Define `perimeter` as an **arrow function** stored in a `const`, using a concise body with an implicit return. `perimeter(width, height)` returns `2 * (width + height)`, so `perimeter(3, 4)` returns `14`.
guided-practice.starterCode: const perimeter = (width, height) => 0;
guided-practice.solution: const perimeter = (width, height) => 2 * (width + height);
guided-practice.hint: One expression after the arrow, no braces and no return keyword.
guided-practice.explain: Two parameters means the parentheses are compulsory, but the braces are not - and leaving them off is what buys you the implicit return. The parentheses around `width + height` are ordinary arithmetic grouping and have nothing to do with the arrow.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.answer:
Hello, Mira
Welcome, Mira
Hello, Mira
null, Mira
guided-practice.explain: A default fires on exactly one condition: the argument is `undefined`. `null` is something you deliberately passed, so it is used as-is and concatenates as the text `null` - which is why a null arriving from real data looks like a broken default but is not one.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `ovenTime(layerCount, minutesPerLayer)` returning `layerCount * minutesPerLayer`. When `minutesPerLayer` is not supplied, assume `5`. `ovenTime(3)` returns `15`, and a `minutesPerLayer` of `0` must genuinely return `0`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
function ovenTime(layerCount, minutesPerLayer) {

}
guided-practice.hint: The fallback belongs in the parameter list, written with a single `=`.
guided-practice.explain: A default parameter is not an assignment that runs every call - it runs only when the argument is `undefined`. That is exactly why `0` survives here, unlike the older `minutesPerLayer = minutesPerLayer || 5` trick, which would silently turn a deliberate zero back into five.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Each `let` creates a brand new binding inside its own pair of braces, so three names spelled identically never touch one another. The inner ones shadow the outer for the length of their block and then vanish, leaving the outermost `power` exactly as it started.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these lines into a counter factory: `makeCounter()` must hand back a function that returns 1, then 2, then 3 on successive calls.
guided-practice.explain: The counter's memory has to be created before the inner function is returned, and it has to sit outside that inner function. Slide `let count = 0` one level in and every call would rebuild it, so the counter would answer 1 forever.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `runCounter(times)`. Inside it, build a counter with a closure - a function that starts at 0 and returns one more each time it is called - then call that counter `times` times and return the array of values it produced. `runCounter(3)` returns `[1, 2, 3]` and `runCounter(0)` returns `[]`.
guided-practice.hint: Declare `count` inside makeCounter but outside the function makeCounter returns.
guided-practice.explain: makeCounter returns before the inner function has ever run, yet `count` is still there - the returned function keeps the scope it was born in alive. If `count` were declared inside the returned function instead, it would be rebuilt on every call and the answers would all be 1.

challenge-set.prompt: `applyDiscount(price, percent)` should return the price with that percentage taken off, so `applyDiscount(100, 10)` gives `90`. Every test reports `undefined` instead. Fix it.
challenge-set.solution: const applyDiscount = (price, percent) => price - price * percent / 100;
challenge-set.hint: Look at what the braces after the arrow turned the body into.
challenge-set.explain: Braces after `=>` open a statement body, and statements produce nothing for the caller: the subtraction really happened and was then dropped on the floor. Either add `return` inside the braces or delete the braces so the body is once again a single expression.

challenge-set.prompt: Define `scale` as an arrow function stored in a `const`. `scale(values, factor)` returns a **new** array holding every number in `values` multiplied by `factor`, leaving `values` untouched. `factor` defaults to `2`, so `scale([1, 2, 3])` returns `[2, 4, 6]`.
challenge-set.hint: This arrow has a braced body, so it needs an explicit return - and the default goes in the parameter list.
challenge-set.explain: Two rules from this floor meet here: a braced arrow body must return for itself, and a default only fires on `undefined`, which is why `[5], 0` genuinely scales to zero instead of doubling. Filling a fresh array rather than writing back into `values` is what keeps the caller's data intact.

challenge-set.prompt: Give the value at each point. Write numbers plainly, with no quotes.

steps.label: the parameter `level` inside raise, during the first call, before the addition
the parameter `level` inside raise, during the second call, before the addition
the outer `level`, after both calls have finished

challenge-set.explain: A parameter is just another local binding that happens to be initialised by the caller, and it shadows the outer name for the whole body. Assigning to it rewrites the local copy, so the outer `level` is never touched even though the code reads as if it were being incremented in place.

challenge-set.prompt: `total(values)` should add up the numbers in `values` and return the sum, giving `0` for an empty array. It fails with `sum is not defined`. Move one line to fix it.
challenge-set.hint: Which block does `sum` belong to, and how long does that block last?
challenge-set.explain: A loop body is a fresh block on every pass, so `let sum = 0` created, used and destroyed a new binding each iteration, leaving nothing for the `return` outside the loop to find. An accumulator must be declared in a scope that outlives the loop it accumulates in.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `runningTotals(values)`. Inside it, build an adder with a closure - a function that keeps a private total starting at 0, adds the number it is given, and returns the new total - then feed it each value in order and return the array of totals. `runningTotals([2, 3, 5])` returns `[2, 5, 10]`.
challenge-set.hint: The returned function takes one number; the total it adds to lives one scope out.
challenge-set.explain: The running total lives in makeAdder's scope, where nothing outside the returned function can read or corrupt it - that privacy is the practical reason closures exist. Each call both updates the captured binding and reports it, which is why the result is a history rather than the same number four times.

challenge-set.prompt: `makeCounter` has already returned, so its local `count` should be gone - yet the function it handed back keeps counting up. Explain what keeps `count` alive, and why two counters built by the same factory never share a number.
challenge-set.explain: The inner function holds a reference to the binding itself, not a snapshot of the number, so the scope it came from cannot be discarded while that function is still reachable. Because a fresh scope is created on every call to the factory, `a` and `b` each closed over their own `count` and neither can see the other's.

exam.prompt: Exactly one of these programs runs without throwing. Which?
choices:
console.log(sum(1, 2));
function sum(a, b) { return a + b; }

console.log(sum(1, 2));
const sum = function (a, b) { return a + b; };

console.log(sum(1, 2));
const sum = (a, b) => a + b;
None of them - a function must always be written above the line that calls it.
exam.explain: A function declaration is hoisted whole - name and body are both usable from the top of the scope. A function expression only binds its name when its own line runs, so the other two are still in the temporal dead zone and throw `Cannot access 'sum' before initialization`.

exam.prompt: Which of these define a function that returns `n * 2` when called with `n`?
exam.explain: Parentheses around a single parameter are optional, so the first two are the same function written twice. Braces are not decoration: they switch the body from an expression to a statement list, so the third computes `n * 2` and then returns undefined.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: The default is consulted only for `undefined`, so a deliberate `0` means zero and the loop never runs, leaving the starting `result` of 1. Passing `undefined` by hand is indistinguishable from passing nothing at all, which is the whole rule in one line.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `Hi, Mira`.
exam.template:
const greet = (name, greeting ___ "Hi") ___ greeting + ", " + name;
console.log(greet("Mira"));
exam.explain: A default is a single `=` inside the parameter list and belongs to the parameter, not to the body. The arrow still does its one job of separating the whole parameter list from the expression that gets returned.

exam.prompt: Order these lines into a factory `makeStep(size)` whose returned function adds `size` to a private total and returns the new total on each call.
exam.explain: The inner function closes over two things at once - the local `total` and the parameter `size` - because a parameter is captured exactly like any other binding in that scope. That is how one factory produces steppers of different sizes without ever being told `size` again.

exam.prompt: Write `cookingStatus(timerMinutes)`. It returns `'Lasagna is done.'` when the timer shows `0`, `'Not done, please wait.'` for any other number, and `'You forgot to set the timer.'` when it is called with no argument at all.
exam.starterCode:
function cookingStatus(timerMinutes) {

}

tests.expected: You forgot to set the timer.
You forgot to set the timer.

exam.hint: A parameter nobody supplied holds a value you can test for by name.
exam.explain: A parameter that was never supplied holds `undefined`, and you must compare against it with `===`: a truthiness test would class the perfectly valid `0` as missing and report the lasagna as forgotten rather than done. Returning from the first matching branch removes the need for any `else` at all.

exam.prompt: `countdown(from)` should return an array counting down from `from` to `1`, and `[]` when `from` is `0`. It throws `steps is not defined`. Fix the scoping.
exam.hint: The array has to outlive the block it is filled in.
exam.explain: The array was born inside the `if` block and died with it, so the `return` two lines below named something that no longer existed anywhere. Declaring it in the function's own scope also makes the guard pointless - a loop whose condition is false from the start already yields the empty array.

exam.prompt: Write `stepValues(size, times)`. Inside it, build a factory whose returned function closes over `size`, adds it to a private total and returns the new total. Call that function `times` times and return the array of totals. `stepValues(5, 3)` returns `[5, 10, 15]` and `stepValues(5, 0)` returns `[]`.
exam.hint: makeStep needs no parameter of its own - `size` is already visible from the scope around it.
exam.explain: The innermost function captures two bindings from two different scopes at once, and neither has to be passed in again. Reading an enclosing parameter is the same lookup a closure performs on any outer name - closures are not a special feature bolted on, just ordinary scope that outlives the call that created it.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `cast` declares its own `spell`, so the lookup stops there and never reaches outward. `echo` declares nothing, so the lookup walks out to the enclosing scope - and that outward walk is precisely what a closure freezes in place when a function is returned rather than called on the spot.

exam.prompt: In two or three sentences, say what a function hands back when its body ends without a `return`, and what changes when an arrow function's body is wrapped in braces instead of written as a single expression.
exam.explain: Falling off the end of a body is not an error in JavaScript - it quietly produces `undefined`, which then travels into the caller and breaks something far away. A concise arrow body is an expression whose value is returned for you; braces turn it into a statement list where nothing comes back unless you ask.

sections.title: A Row of Slots
sections.body:
An **array** is an ordered row of values written in square brackets, and one array can hold numbers, strings, or even other arrays.

Every slot has an **index** counting from `0`, so the first item is `xs[0]` and the last is `xs[xs.length - 1]`.

`length` is a property rather than a method - you read it as `xs.length`, with no parentheses.

Reaching for an index that does not exist is not an error in JavaScript: you quietly get `undefined` back, so a bad index shows up much later than the line that caused it.

Assigning to a slot replaces just that value, and it works even on a `const` array, because `const` freezes the **name**, not the contents.

annotations.text: length counts the items; the highest legal index is always one below it.
Index 9 does not exist, and JavaScript answers undefined instead of throwing.
The array was declared const and this still works - const binds the name, not the row of values.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: The last valid index is one below `length`, so `gems[gems.length]` falls off the end. JavaScript never bounds-checks an index for you, which is why that mistake surfaces as an undefined travelling through your program rather than as an error at the point of the bug.

sections.title: Growing and Shrinking
sections.body:
Four methods change an array **in place** at its two ends: `push` and `pop` work at the back, `unshift` and `shift` work at the front.

What each hands back is the part people forget - `push` and `unshift` return the array's **new length**, while `pop` and `shift` return the **item they removed**.

`splice(start, count)` cuts `count` items out from index `start` and returns those items as a new array; any further arguments are inserted where the cut was made.

All five mutate the array they are called on, so there is nothing to assign - the variable you already have sees the change.

annotations.text: push answers with the new length, 4 - not with the item you added.
shift takes from the front and returns the item, so the array shortens from the left.
splice removes one item at index 1 and inserts two in its place; the return value is what came out.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: shift and push at opposite ends are what make an array behave as a queue: one end lets items out, the other lets them in. Notice `q` was never reassigned - both calls edited the array the name already pointed at.

sections.title: Copies, Searches and Spread
sections.body:
`slice(start, end)` is the **pure** twin of `splice`: it copies out a new array from `start` up to but not including `end`, and leaves the original untouched.

Negative arguments count back from the end, so `xs.slice(-2)` is the last two items and `xs.slice(1, -1)` is everything except the two ends.

To search, `indexOf(value)` gives the **first** position of a value or `-1` when it is absent, `lastIndexOf(value)` gives the last, and `includes(value)` answers the same question with `true` or `false`.

The **spread** syntax `...` unpacks one array into another, so `[...xs]` is a fresh copy and `[...a, ...b]` is the two joined - neither original is changed.

Copying is worth the keystrokes because `const b = a` gives two names for **one** array: push through either name and both names see it.

annotations.text: The end index is excluded, so 1 to 3 yields two items, not three.
xs is unchanged - slice copied, it did not cut.
Two 20s in the row, so the first and last positions differ: 1 and 3.
Pushing onto the copy left xs at four items; a plain `const copy = xs` would have shown five.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so the first line prints 1 - the position of "rope" - and the second prints true.
checkpoint.explain: indexOf answers where and includes answers whether, and the distinction bites because the position of a first item is `0`, which is falsy. That is exactly why `if (stock.indexOf(x))` is a bug and `if (stock.includes(x))` is not.

sections.title: map, filter and reduce
sections.body:
These three take a **callback** - a function handed to another function - written here as an arrow function such as `(n) => n * 2`.

`map` builds a new array by transforming every element, so its result is **always the same length** as the input, while `filter` keeps only the elements whose callback returned true, so its result is the same length or shorter.

`reduce(callback, initial)` folds the whole array down to one value: the callback receives the accumulator so far and the current element, and whatever it returns becomes the accumulator for the next element.

That second argument is the starting accumulator, and **omitting it is a trap** - without it JavaScript uses the first element as the accumulator and starts at the second, which silently skews any fold that is not a plain sum and throws a TypeError on an empty array.

All three are pure: the array they are called on is never modified.

annotations.text: One output item per input item - map can never change the length.
filter keeps elements as they are; the callback only decides yes or no.
No initial value, so the accumulator starts as the raw 1 and the multiplication never touches it: 91, not 100.
nums still holds its original four values - all three methods returned new arrays.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: filter hands back the elements themselves while map hands back whatever the callback returned - the same array read two different ways. That is why the filtered array can be shorter than the input and the mapped one never is.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: A three-item array has indices 0, 1 and 2, so the count and the last index are never the same number. Index 3 is one past the end, and JavaScript hands back undefined rather than complaining - the count is the only thing telling you where the row stops.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so "torch" is added to the end of the bag and then taken straight back off. It prints: ["rope"] torch
guided-practice.explain: push and pop are a matched pair at the back of an array: one grows it and returns the new length, the other shrinks it and returns the item. That asymmetry is why `const last = bag.push("torch")` would hand you a number instead of a string.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `lastOf(xs)` returning the final item of the array `xs`, or the string "empty" when `xs` has no items.
guided-practice.hint: The last index is xs.length - 1, and an empty array makes that -1.
guided-practice.explain: The empty case needs its own branch because `xs.length - 1` becomes -1 there, and `xs[-1]` in JavaScript is not the last item - it is a property that does not exist, so you would return undefined without ever seeing an error.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: The two calls return different kinds of thing: push reports the array's new size, shift reports the value it took away. Both edited `q` itself, which is why the final line shows the leftovers of two operations rather than the array you wrote down.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `withoutEnds(xs)` returning a **new** array holding everything except the first and last items. `withoutEnds([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])` is `[2, 3, 4]`, and an array of two items or fewer gives back an empty array.
guided-practice.hint: A negative end index counts back from the end of the array.
guided-practice.explain: slice clamps bounds that overshoot instead of throwing, so the short arrays fall out for free with no length check. It also copies, which means the caller's array survives - the same job written with splice would have destroyed it.

guided-practice.prompt: `hasRune(runes, rune)` should return `true` when `rune` is somewhere in `runes` and `false` otherwise. It gets the first item wrong. Fix it.
guided-practice.hint: indexOf reports -1 for absent, and 0 is a perfectly good position.
guided-practice.explain: The absent marker is -1, not 0, so the only safe comparisons are `>= 0` or `!== -1` - `> 0` throws away the first slot. includes sidesteps the arithmetic entirely by answering with a boolean, which is what the caller wanted in the first place.

challenge-set.prompt: What does this print?
challenge-set.explain: splice returns what it removed and edits the array in place, so the value you get and the array you kept are two different halves of one operation. A count of 0 removes nothing, which turns the same call into a pure insertion.

challenge-set.prompt: Two calls that look alike do very different things. Trace each value as it is created.
challenge-set.explain: slice reads two indices - a start and an excluded end - while splice reads a start and a count, which is why the same numbers produce two items and then three. Only the second call leaves a mark: the array itself is shorter afterwards.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `evenSquares(xs)` returning a new array holding the square of each **even** number in `xs`, in the original order. `evenSquares([1, 2, 3, 4])` is `[4, 16]`.
challenge-set.hint: filter returns an array, so you can call .map straight onto it.
challenge-set.explain: Filtering before mapping keeps the transform simple, because map is then left with nothing to decide - each stage does one job and hands an array to the next. Doing it the other way round would square the odd numbers too and leave you testing squares for evenness.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `longestWord(words)` returning the longest string in `words`. When two are equally long keep the earlier one, and an empty array returns the empty string "".
challenge-set.hint: Start the accumulator at "" - every real word beats it.
challenge-set.explain: The initial value doubles as the answer for the empty array, so the required behaviour costs no extra branch. Comparing with `>` rather than `>=` is what keeps the earlier of two equal-length words, because a tie leaves the accumulator alone.

challenge-set.prompt: `sumOfDoubles(xs)` should double every number and add the results together, so `sumOfDoubles([3, 4])` is 14. It returns 11 instead, and throws on an empty array. Fix it.
challenge-set.hint: reduce takes a second argument after the callback.
challenge-set.explain: With no initial value the first element becomes the accumulator untouched, so 3 is added raw and only 4 is ever doubled - the fold silently skips its own first step. Supplying 0 also gives the empty array an answer, which is why it stops throwing.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `addSpare(xs, item)` returning a two-element array: first a **new** array holding everything in `xs` followed by `item`, then `xs.length` read afterwards. Because `xs` must be left untouched, that second number is its original length. `addSpare([1, 2], 3)` is `[[1, 2, 3], 2]`.
challenge-set.hint: [...xs, item] builds a new row without disturbing the old one.
challenge-set.explain: Spreading copies the values into a brand-new array, so the caller's array keeps its length - that reported length is exactly the test a push-based answer fails. Reaching for push here would edit an array you were only lent, which is the quiet way one function breaks another.

challenge-set.prompt: What does this print?
challenge-set.explain: `const b = a` copies a reference, not a row of values, so `a` and `b` are two names for one array and a push through either is visible through both. The spread in `c` is what actually duplicates the contents, which is why it stayed at two items.

exam.prompt: Given `const xs = [10, 20, 30];`, what does `xs[3]` evaluate to?
exam.explain: Indices run from 0 to length - 1, and reading past the end is legal in JavaScript: a missing slot is just a missing property, which reads as undefined. Nothing is raised, so nothing marks the spot where the mistake was made.

exam.prompt: Which call removes the **first** item of `xs` and returns that item?
exam.explain: shift is the front-end counterpart of pop. unshift travels the other way - it inserts at the front and returns a length - and slice removes nothing at all, because it copies rather than cuts.

exam.prompt: Which of these leave the original array `xs` unchanged?
exam.explain: slice and spread each build a new array and hand it back, while splice and push edit in place and return something else entirely - removed items and a new length. Whether a call yields an array is not the tell; whether it names a new one is.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: Both searches report positions, and with a repeated value they disagree on purpose - first match against last. The absent value gives -1 from indexOf and false from includes, two ways of saying the same thing, and only one of them is safe to drop straight into a condition.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints 9 - the sum of the three numbers.
exam.template:
const total = [2, 3, 4].___((acc, n) => acc ___ n, 0);
console.log(total);
exam.explain: reduce is the fold that turns many values into one, and the `0` after the callback is the accumulator it starts from. The callback's only job is to say how the next element joins what has been gathered so far.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: For a plain sum the missing initial value happens to be harmless, because the first element is exactly what you would have started from anyway. It is not decoration though - it fixes the starting point, and it is the only thing that gives an empty array an answer instead of a TypeError.

exam.prompt: A colleague writes `sum(xs)` as `xs.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n)`. It works on `[10, 20]`, but throws `TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value` on `[]`, and their character counter `words.reduce((acc, s) => acc + s.length)` returns the string "a1" for `["a", "b"]`. Explain what the missing second argument does and why supplying it fixes both.
exam.explain: Without an initial value reduce borrows the first element as the accumulator and starts folding at the second, so the accumulator inherits that element's type - a string, in the counter - and the first element never passes through the callback at all. An empty array has no first element to borrow, which is the TypeError. Passing 0 fixes both at once: the accumulator is a number from the start, every element is folded, and the empty case returns the identity value.

exam.prompt: Arrange these fragments into a function that keeps the positive numbers, doubles them, and returns their total.
exam.explain: Each stage consumes the array the stage before it produced, so the order is forced by the data rather than by taste: you cannot double what has not been selected, and reduce needs the doubled values to add up. Only the last stage stops returning an array, which is why it is the one that can return a total.

exam.prompt: Write `flatten(rows)` where `rows` is an array of arrays, returning one array holding every inner item in order. `flatten([[1, 2], [3]])` is `[1, 2, 3]`.
exam.hint: The accumulator starts as [] and each step spreads one row into it.
exam.explain: The accumulator here is an array rather than a number, which is what makes the initial `[]` essential - without it the first row would become the accumulator and an empty `rows` would throw. Spreading `row` is what stops the result being an array of arrays: pushing the row itself would add one item, not its contents.

exam.prompt: `onlyLong(words, n)` should return the words with **more than** `n` characters. Instead it returns an array of `true` and `false`. Fix it.
exam.hint: The callback is already right - the method around it is not.
exam.explain: map replaces each element with whatever the callback returned, so a boolean test used with map gives you the answers instead of the items. filter runs the identical callback but treats its result as a verdict and keeps the element - same test, a different question asked of it.

exam.prompt: Write `nextInLine(queue)` that moves the front item of `queue` to the back **in place** and returns that same array. `nextInLine([1, 2, 3])` is `[2, 3, 1]`, and an empty queue comes back empty.
exam.hint: shift hands you the item it removed, so it can be passed straight to push.
exam.explain: shift returns the removed item, which is precisely what push needs, so the rotation is a single expression. The empty case has to be guarded because shift on an empty array returns undefined and push would then dutifully store it, leaving a one-item array where you expected none.

sections.title: Objects Are Named Slots
sections.body:
An **object** stores values under names instead of positions. You read a property with dot notation when you know the name, and with brackets when the name is itself a value.

`Object.keys`, `Object.values` and `Object.entries` turn an object back into arrays, which is how you get from a record to something you can `map` over.

A missing property is `undefined` rather than an error - which is convenient until it hides a typo.

annotations.text: No such property, so undefined - not a crash. A misspelt key looks exactly like this.
entries gives [key, value] pairs, ready to map or filter.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `titleOf(book)` returning the book's `title` property.
checkpoint.explain: Dot access reads the slot by name. The empty-string case matters because `''` is falsy - anything that tests the value rather than returning it would quietly get this wrong.

sections.title: Destructuring Pulls Values Out
sections.body:
**Destructuring** unpacks properties into variables in one step, so you name what you need once instead of repeating the object.

You can rename with `:`, supply a default with `=` for when a property is missing, and collect whatever is left with `...rest`.

A default fires only for `undefined` - a property that is present and `null` keeps its `null`.

annotations.text: port is present so 8080 wins; mode is absent so the default applies.
tls is null, not undefined, so the default does NOT fire.
Arrays destructure by position, and defaults work the same way.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Defaults are triggered by `undefined` alone. `null` is a value someone chose, so destructuring leaves it in place - which is the whole reason `??` exists.

sections.title: Reaching Into Nested Data Safely
sections.body:
Real data is nested and often incomplete. `a.b.c` throws the moment `a.b` is undefined, which turns one missing field into a crash.

**Optional chaining** `?.` stops and yields `undefined` instead of throwing. It works on properties, array indexes with `?.[i]` and calls with `?.()`.

It short-circuits: once the left side is nullish, nothing further is evaluated.

annotations.text: contact is missing, so the whole expression is undefined rather than a TypeError.
?.() calls the function only if it exists.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `cityOf(user)` returning `user.address.city`, or the string `"unknown"` if either the address or the city is missing. It must not throw.
checkpoint.explain: One `?.` guards the whole chain because it short-circuits, and `??` turns the resulting undefined into a value the caller can actually use. Returning undefined would push the missing-data problem downstream.

sections.title: Defaults That Respect Zero
sections.body:
`||` falls back whenever the left side is **falsy**, which includes `0`, `""` and `false` - all legitimate values someone may have chosen.

`??` falls back only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. That distinction is the difference between a setting of zero being honoured and being silently overwritten.

Reach for `??` for defaults and keep `||` for genuine truthiness tests.

annotations.text: 0 is falsy, so || throws away a deliberate setting of zero.
?? keeps the 0 because it is neither null nor undefined.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: This one line is why `??` was added to the language: `||` cannot tell a deliberate zero from an absent value, and volume, counts and coordinates are all legitimately zero.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.code:
const p = { x: 1, y: 2 };
console.log(Object.keys(p).length);
guided-practice.explain: Object.keys returns an array, so length counts the properties. This is the usual way to ask how many keys an object has, since objects have no length of their own.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `countKeys(obj)` returning how many own properties the object has.
guided-practice.starterCode:
function countKeys(obj) {
  
}
guided-practice.explain: A property holding null still exists, so it counts. Object.keys asks about presence, not about whether the value is useful - which is exactly what a count should mean.
guided-practice.hint: Object.keys gives you an array.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this pulls `title` and `year` out of the book in one statement.
guided-practice.explain: Object destructuring mirrors the literal syntax: braces on the left take apart what braces on the right put together.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `fullName(person)` that destructures `first` and `last` and returns them joined by a space. If `last` is missing, use `"Unknown"`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
function fullName(person) {
  
}
guided-practice.explain: The default fires for the absent last name but not for the empty string, because only undefined triggers it. That third test is what separates a default from a truthiness check.
guided-practice.hint: Give last a default inside the braces.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Both chains stop at a nullish link and yield undefined. Without the `?.` the first line would throw, because you cannot read a property of null.

guided-practice.prompt: This should return the configured port, keeping a port of 0 if that is what was set. It does not. Fix it.
guided-practice.explain: `||` treats a port of 0 as absent and replaces it. `??` only replaces null and undefined, so a deliberate zero survives - the exact bug that makes configuration systems ignore what you asked for.
guided-practice.hint: Which operator distinguishes absent from falsy?

guided-practice.prompt: Write `restOf(obj)` that removes the `id` property and returns everything else as a new object, without mutating the original.
guided-practice.starterCode:
function restOf(obj) {
  
}
guided-practice.explain: Rest in destructuring builds a fresh object from what is left, so the caller's data is untouched. Deleting the key with `delete` would work but would mutate an object you do not own.
guided-practice.hint: Destructure id out and collect ...rest.

guided-practice.prompt: Trace the value of `out` as this loop runs over the entries.
guided-practice.explain: Object.entries turns the record into pairs, and destructuring in the loop header names them. Naming the running total at each step is how you catch an accumulator declared inside the loop instead of outside it.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `pluck(records, key)` returning an array of that property from every record. Records missing the key contribute `null`.
challenge-set.starterCode:
function pluck(records, key) {
  
}
challenge-set.explain: Bracket access is required because the key is a value, not a literal name. Mapping missing values to null keeps the output the same length as the input, which anything downstream will assume.
challenge-set.hint: Bracket notation, then ?? null.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `withDefaults(config)` returning a new object where a missing or nullish `host` becomes `"localhost"` and a missing or nullish `port` becomes `8080`. Values already present - including `0` - are kept.
challenge-set.starterCode:
function withDefaults(config) {
  
}
challenge-set.explain: Building a new object rather than assigning into the caller's keeps the function pure. Using `??` per field is what lets port 0 survive while a genuinely absent port still gets a default.
challenge-set.hint: Return an object literal built from ?? expressions.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `deepGet(obj)` returning `obj.data.items[0].name`, or the string `"missing"` if any link in that chain is absent. It must not throw.
challenge-set.starterCode:
function deepGet(obj) {
  
}
challenge-set.explain: Optional chaining handles every missing link, and `??` supplies the fallback once. Writing this with nested ifs takes six lines and one of them is usually forgotten - the empty-array case.
challenge-set.hint: ?. on each link, ?? at the end.

challenge-set.prompt: A colleague replaces every `||` default in a settings module with `??` and a test breaks: an empty search string used to fall back to `"*"` and now does not. Explain what changed and how you would decide which operator each default should use.
challenge-set.explain: Neither operator is correct everywhere. The question to ask per field is whether an empty or zero value is a legitimate choice the user made - if it is, use `??`; if the field is only ever meaningful when non-empty, `||` is the honest one.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `invert(obj)` returning a new object with keys and values swapped. Values are always strings.
challenge-set.starterCode:
function invert(obj) {
  
}
challenge-set.explain: Entries plus bracket assignment is the general shape of any record-to-record transformation. Note that inverting is lossy if two keys share a value - the last one silently wins.
challenge-set.hint: Loop over Object.entries and assign out[v] = k.

challenge-set.prompt: This should return the display label, falling back to the id, and never throw on an incomplete record. Fix it.
challenge-set.explain: The crash and the fallback are two separate bugs: `?.` stops the throw when meta is absent, and `??` supplies the id. Fixing only one of them still fails a third of the tests.
challenge-set.hint: Two operators are missing, not one.

level-project.prompt:
Build a small data transformation pipeline.

`summarise(orders)` takes an array of order records and returns a summary object:

- `count` - how many orders there are
- `total` - the sum of every order's `amount`, treating a missing or nullish amount as 0
- `customers` - an array of unique `customer.name` values, in first-seen order, skipping orders with no customer

An empty input must return `{ count: 0, total: 0, customers: [] }` rather than throwing.

tests.input: [{ amount: 10, customer: { name: 'Mira' } }, { amount: 5, customer: { name: 'Corvin' } }]

level-project.explain: Every idea on this floor earns its place here: `??` keeps a genuine amount of 0 out of the fallback, `?.` survives orders with no customer at all, and first-seen ordering rules out sorting or a bare Set. The empty-input case falls out for free because the accumulators start at their identity values.
level-project.hint: One pass, three accumulators. Watch the amount-of-zero case.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
const { a = 5 } = { a: 0 };
console.log(a);
exam.explain: 0 is present, and defaults only replace undefined, so the default never fires. Reading this as a truthiness test is the most common way to get it wrong.

exam.prompt: Which expression returns `0` when `x` is `0`?
exam.explain: Only `??` distinguishes absent from falsy. The other three all test truthiness in different clothing, and 0 is falsy in every one of them.

exam.prompt: Write `pick(obj, keys)` returning a new object containing only those keys that exist on `obj`.
exam.starterCode:
function pick(obj, keys) {
  
}
exam.explain: `in` asks about presence, which is what the prompt requires - a truthiness check would drop the key holding 0. That third test exists precisely to catch that shortcut.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `?.` turns a null link into undefined instead of a throw, and `??` then turns that undefined into the fallback. The two operators are designed to be used together like this.

exam.prompt: This should return the initials of first and last name, and cope with a missing name object. Fix it.
exam.explain: Each part must degrade independently, which is why one guard around the whole expression is not enough - the third test has a first name but no last, and only per-part fallbacks handle it.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `rest` holds every property except `id`.
exam.explain: The rest element collects what the named bindings did not take. It builds a new object, so the original record is never modified.

exam.prompt: Write `groupCount(items)` returning an object mapping each item's `type` to how many times it appears. Items with no `type` are ignored.
exam.starterCode:
function groupCount(items) {
  
}
