exam.explain: `(out[t] ?? 0) + 1` handles the first sighting and every later one with the same expression, which is why counting rarely needs an if. Skipping untyped items keeps the tally honest rather than inventing an undefined bucket.

exam.prompt: You are handed API data where any field may be absent. Explain why reaching for `?.` everywhere is not automatically the right answer, and when you would rather let the access throw.
exam.explain: Optional chaining converts a loud failure into a quiet undefined that travels onwards and fails somewhere less obvious. Where a field is genuinely required, validating once at the boundary and throwing there gives a far better error than a `?.` chain that yields undefined three functions later.

exam.prompt: Order these so the function returns a copy of the record with its id removed.
exam.explain: The destructuring statement has to run before rest can be returned. Returning first is the kind of ordering slip that reads fine until you notice rest is not yet defined.

exam.prompt: Write `normalise(record)` returning a new object with `name` (defaulting to `"unknown"` when nullish), `score` (defaulting to `0` when nullish), and `city` taken from `record.address.city` or `"n/a"` if unavailable. It must not throw on an empty record.
exam.starterCode:
function normalise(record) {
  
}
exam.explain: The third test is the whole point: an empty name and a score of zero are real values and must survive, while a missing city still needs its fallback. `??` and `?.` together express that in three lines with no branching.

sections.title: A Class Builds Objects
sections.body:
A **class** describes a kind of object, and `new Lantern(10)` runs its **`constructor`** to build one **instance**. Inside the constructor, **`this`** is the object being built, so every property assigned to `this` becomes that instance's own data.

A **method** is a function written in the class body without the `function` keyword, and inside it `this` is the object the method was called on - whatever sits to the left of the dot.

Two instances share the class but never the data: each carries its own `this`, so burning one lantern cannot drain another.

annotations.text: Runs on `new`. It furnishes an object that already exists; it never returns one.
Copies the argument onto this instance, so it outlives the call.
No `function` keyword and no comma between methods - class body syntax, not an object literal.
A second, wholly separate instance with its own fuel.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a class `Counter` whose constructor takes a starting number and stores it as `this.value`, plus a method `bump()` that adds 1 to `this.value` and returns the new value. Then write `countUp(start, times)`, which builds a `Counter`, calls `bump()` that many times, and returns the final value.
checkpoint.explain: The constructor does not create the object - `new` does that, then hands the fresh object to the constructor as `this` to be furnished. Because the running total lives on the instance, `countUp` can call `bump()` in a loop without threading a counter through every call.
checkpoint.hint: `new Counter(start)` gives you the object; the loop only has to call bump().

sections.title: Getters and Static Methods
sections.body:
A **getter** is a method written with `get` in front of its name, and callers read it like a plain property - `purse.total`, never `purse.total()`. Its body runs on every read, which is how a class exposes a derived value that can never go stale.

A **static** method belongs to the class itself rather than to any instance: `Purse.empty()` works, while `somePurse.empty` is `undefined`.

Statics are the natural home for factory functions that build instances and for helpers that need no instance state at all.

annotations.text: `get` turns this method into a property read. Callers write `found.total`, with no parentheses.
Attached to the class, not to instances - a factory that hands back a new Purse.
The getter recomputes on the next read, so the total cannot drift out of date.
`function` then `undefined`: a static is not reachable through an instance.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a class `Shelf` whose constructor takes an array and stores it as `this.books`, with a getter `count` returning how many books it holds and a static method `blank()` returning a new empty `Shelf`. Then write `shelfSizes(books)` returning the array `[shelf.count, Shelf.blank().count]` for a `Shelf` built from `books`.
checkpoint.explain: `shelf.count` has no parentheses because a getter is read, not called - add them and you try to call the number the getter returned. `blank` sits on the class because building an empty Shelf needs no existing Shelf to start from.
checkpoint.hint: `get count() { ... }` inside the body; `static blank() { return new Shelf([]); }` beside it.

sections.title: extends and super
sections.body:
`class Wand extends Tool` declares that every Wand **is a** Tool and inherits its methods without copying them. A subclass constructor must call **`super(...)`** before it touches `this`: that call runs the parent constructor on the same object, and reading `this` first throws a `ReferenceError`.

Inside a method, **`super.describe()`** reaches the parent's version of a method the subclass has overridden, which lets a subclass extend behaviour instead of replacing it.

`instanceof` answers `true` for every class in the line of descent, because the link between them is a real one and not a copy.

annotations.text: Every Wand is also a Tool, and gets Tool's methods for free.
Must come before any use of `this`, and it runs Tool's constructor on this same object.
Calls the parent's version of the method this class just overrode.
true, true, false - descent runs one way only.

checkpoint.prompt: The `Coin` class is given. Write `class Gem extends Coin` whose constructor takes `(value, purity)`, passes `value` to `super`, stores `this.purity`, and overrides `worth()` to return `super.worth() * this.purity`. Then write `gemWorth(value, purity)` returning `new Gem(value, purity).worth()`.
checkpoint.explain: `super.worth()` runs the parent's method with `this` still pointing at the Gem, so the override wraps inherited behaviour instead of duplicating it. Rewrite the parent's formula by hand and the two copies drift apart the first time one of them changes.
checkpoint.hint: super(value) first, then this.purity; inside worth(), start from super.worth().

sections.title: The Prototype Chain, and What `this` Binds To
sections.body:
A class is sugar over prototypes: a method written in the class body is not copied onto each instance, it lives on `Bell.prototype`, and every instance holds a hidden link to that object. Reading `bell.ring` looks on the instance first, then follows the link to `Bell.prototype`, then to `Object.prototype` - that walk is the **prototype chain**.

The chain explains `this` too. A method has no owner of its own: `this` is whatever object sits to the left of the dot **at the moment of the call**, so `bell.ring()` binds `this` to `bell` while `const loose = bell.ring; loose()` binds nothing and `this` is `undefined`.

An **arrow function** has no `this` of its own at all - it borrows the `this` of the scope it was written in, which is why an arrow assigned to a field in the constructor stays attached to that instance however it is later called.

annotations.text: An own property of the instance, holding an arrow that captured this constructor's `this`.
false then true: the method is on the prototype, not on the instance.
No object to the left of a dot, so `this` is undefined and reading `this.tone` throws a TypeError.
The arrow ignores how it was called and uses the `this` it closed over.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a class `Tally` whose constructor stores `this.total = start` and also assigns an **arrow function** to `this.add`, taking a number, adding it to `this.total`, and returning the new total. Then write `sumWith(start, numbers)` that builds a `Tally`, pulls the function off with `const add = tally.add;`, calls `add(n)` for each number, and returns `tally.total`.
checkpoint.explain: Write `add` as an ordinary method and this same code throws, because the detached call has no object to its left. The arrow was created inside the constructor, where `this` was the new instance, and it keeps that binding forever - the cost is one function object per instance instead of one shared on the prototype.
checkpoint.hint: The arrow must be created inside the constructor, where `this` is the instance.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Each `new Vial(...)` builds a separate object with its own `drops` hanging off its own `this`, so pouring the red vial cannot reach the blue one. `pour` both mutates and returns, which is why the second line shows the value after the decrement, not before.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so `new Rune("ansuz").show()` returns `"ansuz"`.
guided-practice.explain: The constructor is found by its reserved name, never by being listed first, and the object it furnishes arrives as `this` rather than as a parameter you declare. Drop the `this.` and you assign to a local that vanishes the moment the constructor returns.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a class `Vault` with a constructor taking `gold` and storing it as `this.gold`, a method `deposit(amount)` that adds `amount` to `this.gold`, and a method `balance()` returning the current gold. Then write `runVault(start, deposits)`, which builds a `Vault`, deposits every amount in the array in order, and returns `balance()`.
guided-practice.explain: The running total lives on the object, so the loop never has to carry it - that is the trade a class makes, moving state out of the caller and into the thing the state describes. `deposit` mutates while `balance` only reads, a split that keeps the object's rules in one place.
guided-practice.hint: deposit changes this.gold; balance only returns it.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: A getter is read without parentheses and its body runs on every read, which is why the last line reports 5 rather than the 4 computed earlier. `typeof note.length` is `number`, not `function`, because you never touch the function - you touch what it returns.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a class `Basket` whose constructor takes an array of prices and stores it as `this.prices`, with a getter `total` returning their sum and a getter `size` returning how many prices there are. Then write `basketReport(prices)` returning the array `[basket.total, basket.size]` - read both as properties, never call them.
guided-practice.explain: Storing a `total` field in the constructor would freeze a number that goes wrong the moment `prices` changes; a getter derives it on demand, so there is nothing left to keep in sync. The empty basket is the case worth checking - the sum has to start at 0, not at the first element.
guided-practice.hint: `get total()` and `get size()` in the class body; the caller reads basket.total with no parentheses.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: `merge` is reached through the class, never through an instance, which is exactly what the last line reports: `Ledger.merge` is a function while `one.merge` does not exist. A static that builds and returns a new instance is the standard factory shape, and it leaves both inputs untouched.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a class `Temp` whose constructor takes degrees Celsius and stores `this.c`, a static method `fromF(f)` returning a new `Temp` built from `(f - 32) * 5 / 9`, and a method `celsius()` returning `this.c` rounded with `Math.round`. Then write `readF(f)` returning `Temp.fromF(f).celsius()`.
guided-practice.explain: A class gets exactly one constructor signature, so a second way of building the same object belongs on a static factory whose name says which units it expects. Note `-40`, the point where the two scales cross - a good edge case precisely because it is the one input a swapped formula still gets right.
guided-practice.hint: static fromF(f) { return new Temp(...); } - it returns an instance, it does not set anything on `this`.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these fragments into a `Wand` subclass whose constructor stores both fields without throwing.
guided-practice.explain: `super(name)` has to run before `this.charges = charges`, because in a derived class `this` does not exist until the parent constructor has produced it. Swap those two lines and the engine throws a ReferenceError rather than quietly assigning to nothing.

challenge-set.prompt: `run(0, [1, 2, 3])` should return `6` but returns `NaN`. Fix the class without changing `run`.
challenge-set.explain: `count = count` reassigns the parameter to itself and never touches the object, so `this.count` stays `undefined` and the first `undefined + 1` poisons everything downstream as NaN. JavaScript will not warn you: a missing property reads as `undefined` instead of raising, which is why the symptom surfaces far from the mistake.
challenge-set.hint: Which of the two names refers to the object being built?

challenge-set.prompt: The `Creature` class is given. Write `class Dragon extends Creature` whose constructor takes `(name, hoard)`, passes `name` to `super`, and stores `this.hoard`; override `describe()` to return the parent's description followed by `" guarding "`, the hoard, and `" gold"`. Then `dragonLine("Fafnir", 900)` must return `"Fafnir stirs guarding 900 gold"`.
challenge-set.explain: The override starts from `super.describe()` rather than rebuilding the sentence, so a later change to how a Creature announces itself flows through every Dragon for free. The empty-name case shows the parent's rule surviving untouched: Dragon never inspects `name`, it only extends whatever the parent produced.
challenge-set.hint: super(name) inside the constructor; super.describe() inside the method.

challenge-set.prompt: `heir("Mara", 3)` throws `ReferenceError: Must call super constructor in derived class before accessing 'this'`. Fix `Heir` without changing `Noble` or `heir`; `heir("Mara", 3)` must return `"Lord Mara the 3"`.
challenge-set.explain: In a derived class the object is not produced by `new` at all - the parent constructor produces it, and `super(...)` is what runs it, so before that call there is literally no `this` to assign to. The language makes this a hard error instead of a silent lost write, which is why moving one line fixes it completely.
challenge-set.hint: Only one line has to move, and it is the one that mentions the parent.

challenge-set.prompt: The setup below has just run. Give the value of each expression - `true`, `false`, or the bare word a `typeof` produces.
challenge-set.explain: Methods are never copied onto instances: `oak` owns only what was assigned to it directly, and everything else is found by walking oak -> Wand.prototype -> Tool.prototype -> Object.prototype. `extends` is precisely the act of linking those two prototype objects, which is why `oak.use` resolves even though nothing named `use` exists on `oak` or on `Wand.prototype`.

challenge-set.prompt: A team pulls a class method into a variable to use as a callback - `const tick = clock.tick;` then `[1, 2, 3].forEach(tick);` - and every call throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. Explain what `this` is bound to in `clock.tick()` versus in `tick()`, and why assigning an arrow function to `this.tick` inside the constructor fixes it.
challenge-set.explain: Both facts follow from one rule: a method is not owned by the object it was found on, so `this` is decided by the call, not by the definition. `clock.tick()` has `clock` to the left of the dot and binds it; `tick()` has nothing, and class bodies are always strict mode, so `this` is `undefined` rather than the global object. An arrow has no `this` slot of its own, so it keeps whatever `this` was in scope when it was created - the instance, if it was created in the constructor.

challenge-set.prompt: Write a class `Scaler` whose constructor takes a number `factor` and stores it as `this.factor`, plus a method `scaleAll(numbers)` returning a new array with every number multiplied by `this.factor`. `scaleAll` must build the result with `numbers.map(...)`, and the callback it passes to `map` must still see the right `this`. Then write `scaleWith(factor, numbers)` returning `new Scaler(factor).scaleAll(numbers)`.
challenge-set.explain: `map` calls your callback with no receiver, so an ordinary `function (n) { return n * this.factor; }` would see `this` as `undefined` and throw. An arrow has no `this` of its own and reads the one belonging to `scaleAll`, which is the instance - this is the everyday reason arrows are the default shape for callbacks written inside methods.
challenge-set.hint: An arrow callback inherits `this` from scaleAll; a `function` expression does not.

challenge-set.prompt: Fill the blanks so `Blade` inherits from `Weapon` and extends the parent's description instead of replacing it.
challenge-set.explain: `super` wears two hats: called as a function it runs the parent constructor, and used as an object it reaches the parent's methods. Both exist only because `extends` linked the two prototypes in the first place - without it there is no parent to reach.

challenge-set.prompt: The `Pack` class is given, with a getter `weight` returning `this.items.length * 2`. Write `class HeavyPack extends Pack` whose constructor takes `(items, padding)`, stores `this.padding`, and overrides the getter `weight` to return `super.weight + this.padding`. Give `HeavyPack` a static method `bare(padding)` returning `new HeavyPack([], padding)`. Then write `packWeights(items, padding)` returning `[new HeavyPack(items, padding).weight, HeavyPack.bare(padding).weight]`.
challenge-set.explain: `super.weight` reads the parent's getter with `this` still pointing at the HeavyPack, so the parent counts the subclass's own items - overriding a getter works exactly like overriding a method, minus the parentheses. Statics are inherited by subclasses too, but `bare` belongs on HeavyPack because only HeavyPack knows about the extra argument.
challenge-set.hint: `get weight() { return super.weight + this.padding; }` - no parentheses after super.weight.

exam.prompt: Given `class Bell { ring() { return 1; } }` and `const b = new Bell();`, where does the function `ring` actually live?
choices: On `b` itself, copied in by the constructor when the instance was built
On `Bell.prototype`, shared by every instance and found by walking the prototype chain
On `Bell` itself, which is what `static` means
Nowhere until the first call, when the engine creates it on demand
exam.explain: Class syntax is sugar: method definitions are installed once on the constructor's `prototype` object, and instances reach them through a hidden link. That is why `b.hasOwnProperty("ring")` is `false`, and why one shared function serves a million instances.

exam.prompt: `const b = new Bell("low"); const f = b.ring; f();` - what is `this` inside `ring` during the call `f()`?
choices: The instance `b`, because that is the object the method came from
The class `Bell`, because the method is defined there
`undefined`, because nothing sat to the left of a dot and class bodies are always strict mode
The global object, because an unbound call always falls back to it
exam.explain: `this` is fixed by the call site, not by where the function was written, and pulling a method into a variable throws the receiver away. Class bodies are strict mode whether you ask for it or not, so the old sloppy-mode fallback to the global object never happens - you get `undefined` and a TypeError on the first property read.

exam.prompt: Which of these statements are true?
choices: A getter is read as `obj.size`, with no parentheses
A getter's body runs again on every read
A static method is called on the class, as in `Coin.blank()`
A static method is also available on every instance, as in `myCoin.blank()`
A getter's value is computed once during construction and cached on the instance
exam.explain: A getter is a function dressed as a property: no parentheses, and no caching unless you write the caching yourself. A static lives on the class object and is deliberately absent from instances, which is what makes it the right home for a factory that has no instance to work from yet.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: The getter re-reads `this.cards` each time, so pushing onto the array changes the answer with nobody recomputing a stored field. The last line separates the two worlds: the factory belongs to the class, and the instance it built carries no trace of it.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `new Coin(4).doubled` is `8` and `Coin.blank().value` is `0`.
exam.explain: One keyword decides how a member is reached: `get` moves it from a call to a read, and `static` moves it from the instance to the class. The prompt tells you which is which - `.doubled` has no parentheses, and `blank` is reached through `Coin`, not through a coin.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.answer:
bear roars
cub roars softly
true false
exam.explain: `Cub` declares no constructor, so it inherits the parent's and `new Cub("cub")` still sets `name`. Its `cry` overrides the parent's while calling into it through `super`, and `instanceof` walks the chain upward only, which is why a Cub is a Beast but a Beast is not a Cub.

exam.prompt: `report(["a", "bb"])` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'prefix')`. Fix `Labeller` without changing `report`; `report(["a", "bb"])` must return `["* a", "* bb"]`.
exam.explain: `words.map(this.label)` hands `map` the bare function, and `map` calls it with no receiver, so `this` is `undefined` inside `label`. Wrapping it in an arrow keeps the call as `this.label(word)` - a real method call with the instance to the left of the dot - and the empty-array test still passes because `map` simply never calls it.
exam.hint: Passing this.label loses the receiver. Call it, do not hand it over.

exam.prompt: The `Shape` class is given: it stores a `name`, has `area()` returning `0`, and has `describe()` returning `this.name + " has area " + this.area()`. Write `class Square extends Shape` whose constructor takes `(side)`, passes `"square"` to `super`, stores `this.side`, and overrides `area()` to return the side squared. Then `squareLine(3)` must return `"square has area 9"`.
exam.explain: `describe` was written on `Shape` and never edited, yet it reports the square's real area - because `this.area()` is resolved on the instance at call time and finds the override first. That single fact is what makes inheritance worth having: a parent can call forward into behaviour that did not exist when it was written.
exam.hint: super("square") sets the name for you; only area() needs overriding.

exam.prompt: The setup below has just run. Give the value of each expression, or the name of the exception it throws.
exam.explain: The two functions differ in where they live and in where their `this` comes from: `chime` sits on the prototype and takes `this` from the call site, so detaching it strands it; `chimeArrow` is an own property of the instance holding an arrow that captured `this` when the constructor ran. That is the whole trade - memory per instance in exchange for a binding nothing can knock loose.

exam.prompt: Write a class `Inventory`: the constructor takes an array of `{ name, qty }` objects and stores it as `this.items`; a getter `total` returns the sum of every `qty`; a method `add(name, qty)` appends `{ name, qty }` to `this.items` and returns the new `total`; and a static method `empty()` returns a new `Inventory` holding no items. Then write `stockReport(items, name, qty)`, which builds an `Inventory` from `items`, calls `add(name, qty)`, and returns `[inventory.total, Inventory.empty().total]`.
exam.explain: All four members pull in the same direction: the constructor takes the raw data, the method is the only sanctioned way to change it, the getter derives a number nobody has to keep in step, and the static builds an instance when there is none to start from. `add` can end with `return this.total` because reading a getter inside a method is an ordinary property read on `this`.
exam.hint: add pushes then returns this.total; empty() is static and takes no arguments.

lesson.title: Work That Has Not Finished Yet

sections.title: A Promise Is a Value That Arrives Later
sections.body:
A **promise** stands for a value that is not ready yet. It is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled with a value, or rejected with a reason.

`Promise.resolve(v)` gives you one that is already fulfilled, which is all you need to reason about ordering without waiting for anything real.

You read the value with `.then`, and crucially the promise itself is **not** the value - printing it shows a Promise, not what is inside.

annotations.text: A promise is just an object with a then method.
This prints BEFORE the value: .then always runs later, even when the promise is already resolved.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: A `.then` callback is queued as a microtask and cannot run until the synchronous code finishes. Already-resolved makes no difference - the ordering is a rule about the queue, not about waiting.

sections.title: async and await Read Like Ordinary Code
sections.body:
An `async` function always returns a promise, whatever you write inside it. Returning `5` produces a promise fulfilled with `5`.

`await` pauses that function until the promise settles and gives you the plain value, so asynchronous code reads top to bottom.

Awaiting a non-promise is legal and simply yields the value - which is why a function can await something that is sometimes a promise and sometimes not.

annotations.text: await on a plain number works fine and just hands the number back.
The returned 5 becomes a promise fulfilled with 5, not a bare 5.

checkpoint.prompt: Write an `async` function `doubled(n)` that returns `n * 2`.
checkpoint.explain: The `async` keyword wraps the returned value in a promise automatically, so no explicit Promise construction is needed. The tests await the result, which is why a plain return is enough.
checkpoint.hint1: Just return the product - async does the wrapping.

sections.title: Failure Travels Through the Chain
sections.body:
A rejected promise behaves like a thrown error that has not landed yet. Inside an `async` function, `await` on a rejected promise **throws**, so `try`/`catch` works exactly as it does for synchronous code.

Throwing inside an `async` function rejects its promise rather than crashing the caller.

An error that nobody catches becomes an unhandled rejection - silent in many runtimes, which is what makes swallowing them dangerous.

annotations.text: A throw inside async rejects the returned promise; it does not crash here.
await re-throws that rejection, so the catch below sees it.

checkpoint.prompt: Write an `async` function `safeParse(fn)` that awaits `fn()` and returns its value, or returns the string `"failed"` if it rejects or throws.
checkpoint.explain: `try`/`catch` around an `await` catches both a rejected promise and a synchronous throw, because await converts the rejection into a throw at that point. Note `return await` rather than `return` - without the await the try block exits before the promise settles and the catch never fires.
checkpoint.hint2: Make sure you await INSIDE the try.

sections.title: Waiting on Several Things at Once
sections.body:
Awaiting in a loop runs the work one after another. `Promise.all` takes an array of promises and gives you one promise for an array of results, letting them settle together.

`Promise.all` rejects as soon as any single input rejects, discarding the rest. `Promise.allSettled` never rejects: it reports every outcome as `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }`.

Choose `all` when any failure ruins the batch, and `allSettled` when you want to know what did work.

annotations.text: Plain values are allowed alongside promises and come through unchanged.
allSettled reports both outcomes instead of rejecting on the first failure.

checkpoint.prompt: Write an `async` function `sumAll(promises)` that awaits every promise in the array and returns the sum of their values. An empty array returns 0.
checkpoint.explain: `Promise.all` on an empty array resolves immediately to `[]`, so the empty case needs no special branch. The initial value of 0 in reduce is what makes that fall out correctly.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Synchronous statements run to completion first; the microtask queue is drained afterwards. This ordering holds no matter how quickly the promise resolves.

guided-practice.prompt: Write an `async` function `identity(v)` that returns the value it is given.
guided-practice.starterCode:
async function identity(v) {
  
}
guided-practice.explain: Even this trivial function returns a promise rather than the value - which is exactly why callers must await it. The null case confirms that async wraps any value, not just truthy ones.
guided-practice.hint: async does the wrapping for you.

guided-practice.prompt: Write an `async` function `firstValue(promises)` that returns the value of the first promise in the array, or `null` if the array is empty.
guided-practice.starterCode:
async function firstValue(promises) {
  
}
guided-practice.explain: The empty case must be handled before indexing, since awaiting `undefined` would yield undefined rather than null. The third test guards against writing a truthiness check that would turn a resolved 0 into null.
guided-practice.hint: Guard the empty array first.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this waits for both promises together and returns their sum.
guided-practice.explain: `Promise.all` returns a single promise for an array of results, so one await covers both. Awaiting each in turn would also work but would run them one after another instead of together.

guided-practice.prompt: Write an `async` function `withFallback(p, fallback)` returning the resolved value of `p`, or `fallback` if `p` rejects.
guided-practice.starterCode:
async function withFallback(p, fallback) {
  
}
guided-practice.explain: Only a rejection should trigger the fallback, which is why this is try/catch and not `??`. The third test proves the point: a resolved 0 is a real value and must not be replaced.
guided-practice.hint: try/catch, and await inside the try.

guided-practice.prompt: Trace the printed lines in order as this runs.
guided-practice.explain: Everything before the first `await` runs synchronously, which is why 'one' beats 'two'. The await then yields control even though there is nothing real to wait for, so the rest is queued behind the remaining synchronous code.

debugging.prompt: This should return the sum of the resolved values, but it returns something odd. Fix it.
debugging.explain: Adding promise objects rather than their values produces string concatenation of `[object Promise]`, not a number. The missing `await Promise.all` is the whole bug, and the empty case passes even while broken - which is why one green test proves nothing.

debugging.prompt: This is meant to return `"recovered"` when the operation rejects, but the rejection escapes instead. Fix it.
debugging.explain: `return fn()` hands the promise back and leaves the try block immediately, so when it later rejects there is no longer a catch in scope. Adding `await` keeps the function inside the try until the promise settles. The synchronous-throw test passes either way, which is what makes this bug easy to miss.
debugging.hint: The try block finishes before the promise does.

debugging.prompt: This should report every outcome, resolving to an array of status strings, but it rejects as soon as one input fails. Fix it.
debugging.explain: `Promise.all` is all-or-nothing by design, so the first rejection discards every other result. `allSettled` is the tool when partial success is still useful information.
debugging.hint: One of these combinators never rejects.

challenge-set.prompt: Write an `async` function `mapAsync(values, fn)` that applies `fn` to every value, awaits all the results together, and returns them as an array. `fn` may be async or plain.
challenge-set.starterCode:
async function mapAsync(values, fn) {
  
}
challenge-set.explain: `Promise.all` accepts plain values as well as promises, which is why the same code works whether `fn` is async or not. Mapping first and awaiting once runs the work together, where awaiting inside the map callback would serialise it.
challenge-set.hint: map to promises, then Promise.all.

challenge-set.prompt: Write an `async` function `settleCounts(promises)` returning `{ fulfilled, rejected }` counting how many settled each way. It must never reject.
challenge-set.starterCode:
async function settleCounts(promises) {
  
}
challenge-set.explain: The promise `settleCounts` returns must resolve even when every input rejected, so `allSettled` is the only combinator that fits the contract. Counting from its status field avoids any try/catch entirely.
challenge-set.hint: allSettled gives you a status per entry.

challenge-set.prompt: Write an `async` function `retry(fn, attempts)` that calls `fn()` up to `attempts` times, returning the first resolved value. If every attempt rejects, return the string `"gave up"`. `fn` receives the attempt number, starting at 1.
challenge-set.starterCode:
async function retry(fn, attempts) {
  
}

tests.input: async n => { if (n < 3) throw new Error('no'); return n; }, 3

challenge-set.explain: The loop must await inside the try so a rejection is caught rather than escaping, and the success path returns immediately rather than continuing to retry. The second test confirms the attempt number is passed through, which is what makes conditional retry logic testable at all.
challenge-set.hint: Loop, try/catch, return on the first success.

challenge-set.prompt: A function awaits ten independent requests inside a `for` loop and is slow. Explain why, and what you would change - including when the loop is actually the correct choice.
challenge-set.explain: Awaiting inside a loop makes each call wait for the previous one, so total time is the sum rather than the maximum. `Promise.all` fixes it when the calls are independent - but a loop is right when each call depends on the previous result, or when you are deliberately rate-limiting.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: An async function returns a promise, and `typeof` a promise is 'object'. The value only appears once the microtask queue runs, which is why it prints second.

exam.prompt: Which combinator resolves with every outcome even when some inputs reject?
exam.explain: `all` rejects on the first failure and `race` settles with whichever finishes first. Only `allSettled` promises to report on every input regardless of outcome.

exam.prompt: Write an `async` function `chain(value, fns)` that passes the value through each async function in turn, awaiting each before the next, and returns the final result.
exam.starterCode:
async function chain(value, fns) {
  
}
exam.explain: This is the case where a loop with an await is correct rather than wasteful: each step needs the previous result, so they genuinely cannot run together. The empty-array case returns the input untouched, which falls out of the accumulator naturally.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: A throw inside an async function rejects its promise instead of propagating synchronously, so the surrounding code keeps running and the handler fires later from the microtask queue.

exam.prompt: This should return an array of resolved values but returns an array of promises. Fix it.
exam.explain: Mapping over promises produces promises - the array is the wrong shape, not the wrong length. `Promise.all` is what converts an array of promises into a promise of an array.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so a rejection is caught and reported.
exam.explain: Because `await` turns a rejection into a throw at that line, ordinary try/catch is the right tool - there is no separate asynchronous error syntax to learn.

exam.prompt: Write an `async` function `firstSuccess(fns)` that calls each function in order and returns the first value that resolves, or `null` if all of them reject.
exam.starterCode:
async function firstSuccess(fns) {
  
}
exam.explain: Returning inside the try exits on the first success, and the catch deliberately does nothing so the loop continues. Falling off the end means every attempt failed, which is the only path that reaches the null.

exam.prompt: Trace the order of the printed lines.
exam.explain: All synchronous work drains first (1, 2, 5), then microtasks run in the order they were queued - the `.then` was registered before the async function hit its await, so 3 precedes 4.

exam.prompt: Why is an unhandled promise rejection more dangerous than an uncaught synchronous exception?
exam.explain: A synchronous throw stops the code immediately and is impossible to ignore. A rejected promise nobody handles often produces only a warning while the program carries on with missing data, so the real failure surfaces far from its cause.

exam.prompt: Write an `async` function `batchTotal(promises)` that sums the values of the promises that resolve, ignoring any that reject. An empty array returns 0.
exam.starterCode:
async function batchTotal(promises) {
  
}
exam.explain: This combines the whole floor: partial failure must not abort the batch, so `allSettled` is required, and reading `value` only from fulfilled entries avoids adding `undefined` into the total. `Promise.all` would reject on the first failure and return nothing at all.

sections.title: A Function Plus the Scope It Was Born In
sections.body:
A **closure** is a function together with the scope it was created in. When `makeCounter` returns, its local `count` does not vanish - the returned function still holds that **binding**, so the value survives from one call to the next and nothing outside can reach it.

Every call to the factory builds a **fresh** scope, so two counters never share a total, and `typeof count` out in the open answers `undefined` because no such name exists there.

This is the module pattern: private state behind a public function. Real JavaScript files also get privacy from `import`/`export` modules, but this dungeon's worker has no module system at all, so every example on this floor builds its privacy out of closures alone.

annotations.text: count lives in makeCounter's scope. The returned function never copies it - it keeps the binding.
A second call to the factory makes a second scope, so b's count starts at 10 and a's is untouched.
typeof on a name that was never declared answers 'undefined' instead of throwing - proof that count is unreachable from out here.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: Both methods in the returned object close over the same `items`, which is how two functions share private state that no caller can name. The second line is 0 because calling the factory again builds a new scope rather than handing back another view of the old one.

sections.title: The Loop That Only Ever Had One Variable
sections.body:
`var` is function-scoped: the loop has **one** `i` binding and every function created in the body captures that same one. By the time those functions run the loop is over and the single `i` holds its final value, which is why all three answer `3`.

`let` creates a **new binding on each iteration** and carries the previous value into it, so each closure ends up holding its own `j`. The bug was never that closures read the variable too late - it is that `var` only ever gave them one variable to read.

Before `let` existed the fix was to wrap the loop body in an immediately-called function so each pass got a scope of its own; `let` now does that for you.

annotations.text: One binding for the whole loop. All three arrow functions capture it, not its value at the time.
let re-binds j on every iteration, so the three closures capture three separate variables.
i is still readable after the loop - a var belongs to the enclosing function, not to the loop.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? The outer loop uses `var` and the inner one uses `let`.
checkpoint.explain: Every closure reads the one shared `i`, which stopped at 3 when the outer loop ended, but each keeps its own `j` from the iteration that created it. Mixing the two keywords in one nest puts the difference in a single line of output: the tens digit is frozen at the end state, the units digit is not.

sections.title: Factories, Partial Application, Currying
sections.body:
A **function factory** is a function whose product is another function: the arguments you hand the factory become the fixed part of the job, and the arguments you hand the result become the part that varies.

**Partial application** is that idea generalised - supply some arguments now, get back a function waiting for the rest. **Currying** takes it to the limit: a chain of one-argument functions, so `scaleBy(2)` is a reusable doubler and `scaleBy(2)(7)` is the whole job in one line.

Fixing arguments early is what lets you pass a ready-made one-argument function straight to `map` or `filter` instead of writing a fresh wrapper at every call site.

annotations.text: Two arrows means two calls: scaleBy(2) returns a function that has closed over factor.
fixed came from the factory call and rest from the eventual call - the closure is what keeps fixed alive in between.
scaleBy(3) is evaluated once, before the mapping starts, and map reuses that one specialised function.

checkpoint.prompt: Finish `makeGreeter(greeting)` so it returns a function taking a name and returning `greeting + ", " + name`. `greetAll` is written for you and hands your factory's product straight to `map`, so `greetAll("hi", ["ash"])` gives `["hi, ash"]`.
checkpoint.explain: The greeting is fixed once, outside the loop, and the name varies per call - that split is the entire point of a factory. It also keeps the function handed to `map` unary, so the index `map` passes as a second argument cannot quietly become part of the greeting.

sections.title: Pipelines, Caches, and Not Mutating Anything
sections.body:
**Composition** builds one big transform out of small ones: `compose(f, g)` returns `x => f(g(x))`, so the right-hand function runs first and the chain reads right to left. Each stage takes a value and returns a new one, which is what lets you reorder, reuse or drop a stage without reading inside any of them.

`map` and `filter` fit that shape because they return **new** arrays, while `push`, `sort` and `splice` edit the array you gave them - and a stage that edits its input silently changes what every other holder of that array sees.

A **memoised** function closes over a cache, so a repeated argument is answered from memory instead of recomputed. That is only safe while the function is pure: if the same input can produce a different answer, or the input is mutated behind the cache's back, the cache is now confidently wrong.

annotations.text: Right to left: g runs first, then f. compose(names, active) therefore filters, then maps.
Still 2 - filter and map read rows and build new arrays rather than editing this one.
The cache is created once, in memoise's scope, and shared by every call to the returned function.
This line runs only on a miss, which is how you can watch the cache work: 4 is computed once and answered twice.

checkpoint.prompt: Finish `triple` inside `countedTriple(inputs)`. It answers a repeated number from `cache`, and otherwise computes `n * 3`, stores it, and adds one to `misses`. `countedTriple([2, 2, 5])` returns `[[6, 6, 15], 2]`.
checkpoint.explain: `misses` and `cache` both live outside the arrow function and both outlive every individual call to it - a memoised function is just a closure with a lookup table inside. Counting misses rather than results is the only way to see a cache at all, because a correct cache changes the work done and never the answer given.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: `first` and `second` were made by two separate calls, so they hold two separate `total` bindings and neither can disturb the other. The last line is 8 rather than 0 because adding zero still reads the total that survived from the earlier calls - the variable was never reset, only the scope was never shared.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so the first line prints `0 2` and the second prints `14`.
guided-practice.explain: The first blank has to be `let` because only a per-iteration binding lets `fns[0]` and `fns[2]` disagree; with `var` both would answer 3. The second blank is the factory's own parameter, and it stays alive after `makeAdder` returns precisely because the inner function still refers to it.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `makeAccumulator(start)` so it returns a function that adds its argument to a running total and returns the new total. `runAccumulator` is written for you: it builds one accumulator and feeds it every number in turn, so `runAccumulator(0, [1, 2, 3])` returns `6`.
guided-practice.hint: Declare the total in makeAccumulator's body, not inside the function you return.
guided-practice.explain: The total has to be declared in the factory's body: put it inside the returned function and it is rebuilt from `start` on every call, so nothing accumulates. One factory call means one scope, and that scope is the accumulator's memory - there is no object and no field involved.

guided-practice.prompt: Make `scaleBy(factor)` return a function that multiplies its single argument by `factor`, so `scaleAll(2, [1, 2, 3])` returns `[2, 4, 6]`. Do not change `scaleAll`.
guided-practice.hint: `(factor) => (n) => ...` - the outer call fixes the factor, the inner one does the work.
guided-practice.explain: `scaleBy(factor)` is evaluated once and the resulting one-argument function is what `map` calls, so the factor is fixed before the traversal starts rather than looked up on every element. Passing a multi-argument function to `map` directly is the classic way to get bitten, because `map` also supplies the index and the whole array.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `compose(f, g)` so it returns a function running `g` first and passing that result to `f`. `loudly` uses `compose(exclaim, shout)`, so `loudly("hi")` returns `"HI!"` and not `"HI!"` uppercased after the fact.
guided-practice.hint: Return an arrow taking one value: the inner call is g, the outer call is f.
guided-practice.explain: `compose` reads right to left because that is the order the parentheses would sit in if you wrote `f(g(x))` by hand. Getting it backwards is invisible on symmetric examples and obvious the moment the stages disagree - here the empty-string case still returns `"!"`, which is what a shout of nothing should be.

guided-practice.prompt: Finish `boost(scores, bonus)` so `boosted` is a NEW array holding every score plus the bonus, and the caller's `scores` array is left exactly as it was. `boost([1, 2], 10)` returns `[[11, 12], [1, 2]]`.
guided-practice.hint: `map` hands back a new array; a `for` loop writing into `scores[i]` does not.
guided-practice.explain: A loop that writes back into `scores[i]` would pass a test that only checked the boosted values, and this one catches it by returning the original alongside. The caller kept a reference to that array, so editing it in place changes a value in code you have never read - which is why transformations return new arrays instead.

debugging.prompt: `labelAt(["a", "b", "c"], 0)` should return `"a"`, but every reader returns `undefined`. Fix it by changing one keyword.
debugging.hint: How many `i` variables does this loop actually create, and what is the value of the last one?
debugging.explain: With `var` the loop has a single `i`, and by the time any reader runs it equals `labels.length` - so every reader indexes one past the end and finds `undefined`. `let` gives each iteration its own binding, which is why the fix is one keyword rather than a rewrite: the closures were always correct, the variable they shared was not.

debugging.prompt: `squareRun([2, 2, 3])` should return `[[4, 4, 9], 2]` - the underlying function runs once per distinct input - but it returns `[[4, 4, 9], 3]`. The answers are right and the cache never helps. Fix `memoise`.
debugging.hint: Which scope does the cache need to live in to outlive a single call?
debugging.explain: A cache declared inside the returned function is rebuilt empty on every call, so the lookup always misses and the memoisation is pure overhead. Moving it into `memoise`'s body makes it part of the closure the returned function keeps, which is the only reason the table survives between calls - and note that a wrong cache position never changes an answer, only the work, so no assertion on results alone would have caught this.

debugging.prompt: `tagAll(["a", "b"], "!")` should return `[["a!", "b!"], ["a", "b"]]` - the second entry is the caller's array, untouched - but both entries come back tagged. Fix it.
debugging.hint: `const tagged = names` gives a second name for one array, not a second array.
debugging.explain: Assigning an array to another variable copies the reference, so `tagged` and `names` are the same object and `const` only stops you rebinding the name, never editing the contents. `map` is the fix because it allocates a new array and leaves the source alone, which is what makes a transform safe to drop into a pipeline shared with other code.

debugging.prompt: `settle` is meant to add one and then halve, so `run(4)` should be `2.5`. It returns `3` instead. Fix `compose` without touching `halve`, `addOne` or the call that builds `settle`.
debugging.hint: Write out `f(g(x))` by hand and see which of the two runs first.
debugging.explain: `compose(f, g)` has to mean `f(g(x))`, so the second argument runs first - the broken version reads left to right and quietly builds the opposite pipeline. Halving and adding do not commute, which is why this shows up as a wrong number rather than a crash; with two symmetric stages the same defect would have shipped unnoticed.

challenge-set.prompt: The two gates below are built, then the calls in the table are made in order, top to bottom. Give the value each one returns.
challenge-set.explain: `toggle` and `peek` were created in the same call, so they close over one `open` and `peek` sees whatever `toggle` last did - the object is only a delivery mechanism, the scope is the state. `other` came from a separate call and therefore has a separate `open`, which is why it is still false after two toggles next door.

challenge-set.prompt: A teammate says a closure "takes a snapshot of the variables it uses at the moment it is created". Use `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);` to disprove it: say what the three functions actually hold, why every one of them answers 3, and what changes when `var` becomes `let`.
challenge-set.explain: If closures copied values, three functions created in three iterations would answer 0, 1 and 2 - they answer 3 because `var` gave the whole loop one binding and all three kept a reference to it. `let` does not change what closures do; it changes how many variables exist, creating one per iteration so each closure has its own to hold.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `memoise(fn)`: it returns a function that answers a repeated argument from a cache held in its closure, calling `fn` only once per distinct argument. `report` is written for you and returns `[results, timesFnRan]`, so `report([2, 2, 3])` gives `[[4, 4, 9], 2]`.
challenge-set.hint: Check membership before computing - `if (n in cache)` - and note that a stored 0 is falsy, so `if (cache[n])` would be a bug.
challenge-set.explain: The `-2, 2` case is the interesting one: two distinct inputs with the same answer must still cost two calls, so the cache has to be keyed on the input rather than on the result. Two traps live here - testing `if (cache[n])` treats a cached `0` as a miss, and a plain object turns every key into a string, so a function taking both `1` and `"1"` needs a `Map` instead.

challenge-set.prompt: Nothing is given to you. Write `makeLedger(start)`, a factory returning an object with four methods and no reachable state: `deposit(n)` adds `n` and returns the new balance; `withdraw(n)` returns the balance unchanged when `n` is greater than the balance, otherwise subtracts and returns the new balance; `balance()` returns the current balance; `history()` returns a NEW array of the accepted amounts in order, positive for deposits and negative for withdrawals. Then write `runLedger(start, moves)`: build one ledger, apply each move in order (a number `>= 0` is a deposit of that amount, a negative number is a withdrawal of its magnitude), then push `999` onto the array `history()` handed you and return `[ledger.balance(), ledger.history()]`. A correct ledger is unaffected by that push.
challenge-set.explain: Handing back the internal log directly would let any caller rewrite the ledger's history without going through `withdraw`, so `history()` must copy - privacy is not just about hiding a name, it is about not leaking references to the things that name points at. The refused withdrawal records nothing, and `withdraw` of exactly the balance is allowed, which is the boundary a `>=` test would get wrong.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `pipe(...fns)`: it returns a function that feeds its argument through every function, left to right, so `pipe(a, b)(x)` is `b(a(x))`. `summary` uses it to keep rows scoring at least 50, uppercase their names and join them with `", "`, so a row list of ash/70 and briar/20 gives `"ASH"`.

tests.input: [{ name: "ash", score: 70 }, { name: "briar", score: 20 }, { name: "cinder", score: 50 }]

challenge-set.hint: Loop over `fns`, carrying the value forward - or fold it with `reduce`, which is the same loop written as one expression.
challenge-set.explain: `pipe` is `compose` read the other way round, and teams pick one direction and stick to it because a mixed codebase makes every chain a guessing game. It only works because each stage returns a new value: `filter`, `map` and `join` all hand back fresh data, so no stage can corrupt the input another stage is still holding.

exam.prompt: `makeCounter` declares `let count` and returns a function that increments and returns it. What does the returned function hold on to after `makeCounter` has finished?
choices: A copy of count, taken at the moment the inner function was created
The count binding itself, so every later change is visible through it
Nothing - count is discarded as soon as makeCounter returns
A copy of every variable that existed anywhere in the program at that moment
exam.explain: The scope outlives the call because something still refers to it, and the engine keeps exactly the bindings that are still reachable - not a snapshot of their values. That is why two closures made in the same call can see each other's writes, and why a counter can count at all.

exam.prompt: After `const fns = []; for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);`, what is `fns.map((f) => f())`?
exam.explain: One `var` binding serves the entire loop, and it holds 3 once the condition has failed - the three closures are reading the same finished variable. Swap in `let` and the answer becomes [0, 1, 2] with no other change, because the loop now creates three bindings instead of one.

exam.prompt: Which of these are true of `const add = (a) => (b) => a + b;`?
choices: add(2) returns a function that has closed over a
Calling add(2) twice makes two functions that share one a
exam.explain: A curried function takes its arguments one call at a time, so the extra argument in `add(2, 3)` is simply ignored and the result is a function, not 5. Each call to `add` also opens a new scope, which is what makes `add(2)` and `add(10)` independent adders rather than two views of one variable.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Note which loop uses `var` and which uses `let`.
exam.explain: The outer `i` is one binding shared by all four closures and it ends at 2, while each inner `j` belongs to its own iteration and keeps 0 or 1. The repetition in the output is the tell: identical pairs mean the outer variable was shared, distinct second halves mean the inner one was not.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so the cache is created once per memoised function and survives between calls. The program prints `36 36` and calls `slow` exactly once.
exam.explain: The cache is named in `memoise`'s scope and referenced from the returned arrow, which is precisely what keeps it alive after `memoise` has returned. The second blank must be the parameter `fn` rather than `slow`: a wrapper that names the wrapped function directly can only ever memoise that one function.

exam.prompt: Order these fragments into a working function factory that prints `15`.
exam.explain: The inner `return` has to sit inside the function being returned, and the factory's own `return` in front of it - two returns at two depths is what a factory looks like. `makeMultiplier(3)(5)` then reads as two calls: the first fixes `factor`, the second supplies `n`.

exam.prompt: A colleague memoises `totalOf(order)`, which sums the numbers in `order.items`. Totals start coming back stale after items are added to an order that was already totalled once. Explain why the cache is now wrong, and state what has to be true of a function - and of the values handed to it - before memoising it is safe.
exam.explain: A cache is a promise that the same input always yields the same answer, and mutating the order breaks that promise while leaving the key looking identical. Memoisation is safe for pure functions over values that nobody edits in place, which is the practical reason functional pipelines return new arrays instead of rewriting the ones they were given.

exam.prompt: `isDigit` fixes `lo` and `hi` and waits for `n`, so `check(5)` should be `true` and `check(10)` `false`. Every call returns `false`. Fix `partial` without changing `between` or the line that builds `isDigit`.
exam.hint: Spread the arguments in the order the target function declares them: the fixed ones came first.
exam.explain: Partial application means the fixed arguments occupy the leading parameters, so spreading `rest` first shifts everything and `between(5, 0, 9)` asks whether 9 lies between 5 and 0. Nothing throws, because JavaScript will happily bind three arguments in any order - the only symptom is an answer that is quietly always false.

exam.prompt: Write `curry3(fn)` so a three-argument function can be called one argument at a time: `curry3(clamp)(0)(10)(42)` is `10`. `clampedRun` is written for you - it fixes `lo` and `hi`, then maps the remaining one-argument function over the numbers.
exam.hint: Three arrows, one per argument, and the innermost body is the only place fn is actually called.
exam.explain: Each arrow closes over the argument given to the one outside it, so by the time the third call happens all three values are still in scope and `fn` can finally run. The payoff is the line in `clampedRun`: bounds are fixed once, and what `map` receives is a plain unary function rather than a wrapper written to capture them.

exam.prompt: Write `composeAll(fns)`: it takes an array of functions and returns a function applying them right to left, so `composeAll([f, g, h])(x)` is `f(g(h(x)))`, and an empty array returns its input unchanged. `describe(numbers, true)` runs evens, then doubled, then total - so `describe([1, 2, 3, 4], true)` is `12` - and `describe(numbers, false)` composes nothing.
exam.hint: Walk the array backwards, carrying the value: the last function in the list is the first to run.
exam.explain: Walking the array backwards is what makes `[total, doubled, evens]` read in the same order as `total(doubled(evens(x)))`, and the empty case has to be the identity function or composition stops being something you can build up from nothing. The stages compose only because each returns a new value - `evens` and `doubled` hand back fresh arrays, so the original list is still intact for any other caller.

sections.title: A Signature Is a Promise
sections.body:
Before the body exists, the **signature** already commits you: what goes in, what comes out, and what happens when the input is wrong.

TypeScript is the usual way to write that down, but it is a compiler, and this floor runs plain JavaScript in a sandbox with no build step. So the contract is written as a JSDoc comment and enforced at runtime instead - the thinking is identical, only the enforcement differs.

Decide the contract first. A function whose failure behaviour you cannot state in one sentence is not designed yet.

annotations.text: The empty case is part of the contract, not an afterthought discovered by a crash.
Because the contract named it, the guard is one line at the top.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `lastOr(xs, fallback)`: it returns the last element of the array, or the fallback when the array is empty. Decide the contract, then write it. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: The third test is the design question in miniature: a last element of 0 is a real answer, so the empty check must be about length rather than about the value being truthy.

sections.title: Validate at the Boundary, Trust Inside
sections.body:
If every function defends against every possible input, the defending is the program. The discipline is to **validate once, at the edge**, and let everything inside assume a clean value.

A boundary check either throws with a message that names the problem, or returns a normalised value. What it must never do is silently continue with something malformed.

The test for a good boundary: after it, can you write the rest without any `if` about shape?

annotations.text: The message names the rule and shows the offending value - that is what makes it debuggable.
Everything downstream now has a real integer and needs no further checking.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `parsePositive(raw)`: convert the input to a number and return it if it is greater than zero. Otherwise throw an `Error` whose message contains the word `invalid`. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Writing the guard as `!(n > 0)` rather than `n <= 0` also rejects NaN, since every comparison with NaN is false. That single detail is the difference between a boundary that holds and one that lets `Number('abc')` straight through.

sections.title: Narrowing Instead of Assuming
sections.body:
When a value may be one of several shapes, **narrowing** is how you find out which, before doing anything that depends on it.

`typeof` distinguishes primitives, `Array.isArray` distinguishes arrays from other objects, and `value === null` has to be checked explicitly because `typeof null` is `"object"`.

Handle each shape in its own branch and the function stays readable. Guess the shape and it fails on the input you did not picture.

annotations.text: null must be first: typeof null is 'object', so a later object branch would claim it.
Arrays are objects too, so isArray has to come before any object handling.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `sizeOf(v)`: return the length for a string or an array, the number of keys for a plain object, and `0` for `null` or `undefined`. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: The order of the branches is the design. Checking nullish first means the object branch never has to wonder about null, and testing arrays before objects keeps `Object.keys` away from a value that has a perfectly good length.

sections.title: One Function, Many Element Types
sections.body:
A utility that works over any array should not care what the elements are. In TypeScript that is a generic; here it is simply a function that never inspects the element itself.

The discipline is to take behaviour as a parameter - a key function, a comparator, a predicate - rather than hard-coding an assumption about the data.

If your utility mentions a property name, it is no longer general.

annotations.text: The caller decides what the key is, so groupBy never mentions a property name.
The same function groups numbers and strings because it never inspects the element.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `uniqueBy(xs, keyFn)`: return the elements whose key is seen for the first time, preserving order. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Deduplicating on the key while returning the original element is what makes this useful for objects, where the elements are never equal but the keys are. A bare `new Set(xs)` would return nothing useful for the third test.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `clampToRange(value, min, max)`. It returns the value constrained to the range. If `min` is greater than `max`, throw an `Error` whose message contains `range`. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: The impossible-range check belongs first, before any clamping, because afterwards there is no sensible answer to return. The degenerate min equals max case is the one people forget, and it must return that single value rather than throw.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `toNumberList(values)`. It takes an array whose elements may be numbers or numeric strings and returns an array of numbers, skipping anything that does not convert to a finite number. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: `Number(null)` is 0 and `Number('')` is 0, so converting first and filtering afterwards silently invents zeroes. Rejecting those inputs before conversion is what makes the fourth test - where genuine zeroes must survive - come out right.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `partition(xs, predicate)`. Return an array of exactly two arrays: the elements for which the predicate is true, then the rest. Order is preserved in both. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: One pass with two accumulators beats calling filter twice, and more importantly it guarantees the two halves partition the input exactly - two independent filters can drift apart if the predicate is not pure.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `safeGet(obj, path, fallback)`. `path` is an array of keys. Walk them in order and return the value found, or the fallback if any step is missing. It must never throw. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: An empty path means no steps were requested, so the object itself is the answer - falling back there would be wrong. The fourth test forces presence checking rather than truthiness, since a stored 0 must be returned rather than replaced by the fallback.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: Both null and arrays report as 'object', which is exactly why narrowing needs an explicit null check and Array.isArray rather than typeof alone.

exam.prompt: Design `countBy(xs, keyFn)` returning an object mapping each key to how many elements produced it. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: Taking the key function as a parameter is what keeps this usable for any element type. `(out[k] || 0) + 1` is safe here because counts are never legitimately falsy once stored.

exam.prompt: Why does `!(n > 0)` reject `NaN` where `n <= 0` does not?
choices: NaN is coerced to 0 by the comparison
Every comparison involving NaN is false, so the negation is true
NaN is less than every number
exam.explain: NaN compares false against everything, including itself. So `NaN > 0` is false and its negation is true, while `NaN <= 0` is also false and lets the value straight through the guard.

exam.prompt: Design `zip(a, b)` returning an array of pairs, stopping at the shorter input. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: Deciding up front to stop at the shorter input is the contract; taking Math.min once expresses it in a single place. Looping to the longer length would silently pair real values with undefined.

exam.prompt: A utility function takes an options object and quietly ignores any key it does not recognise. Argue for and against that choice, then say which you would ship and why.
exam.explain: Ignoring unknown keys keeps callers working across versions, but it turns a misspelt option into behaviour that silently never applies. Rejecting unknown keys catches typos immediately at the cost of brittleness - which is why libraries often warn rather than choosing either extreme.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so the guard rejects both a negative number and NaN.
exam.explain: Negating a positive assertion is what catches NaN, because NaN makes the inner comparison false and the negation therefore true. Writing the negative condition directly would let NaN pass.

exam.prompt: Design `normaliseInput(v)`. Return an array: an array is returned as-is, `null` and `undefined` become `[]`, and any other value becomes a single-element array. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: This is the boundary pattern in one function: after it, every caller can assume an array and stop branching. The fourth test matters because a falsy 0 is a real value that must be wrapped, not discarded.

exam.prompt: Order these so narrowing happens in an order that cannot misclassify a value.
exam.explain: Both null and arrays would be captured by the object branch, so each needs its own test first. Ordering narrowing checks from most specific to most general is the general rule this illustrates.

exam.prompt: You are designing a function before writing its body. What questions do you answer first, and why does answering them first change the code you end up with?
exam.explain: Naming what goes in, what comes out and what happens on invalid input forces the edge cases into the design rather than leaving them to be discovered by a failing test. Functions designed this way tend to have their guards at the top and no defensive checks scattered through the body.

exam.prompt: Design `chunk(xs, size)` splitting the array into consecutive groups of at most `size`. Throw an `Error` containing `size` if `size` is not a positive integer. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: Validating size first is what stops a size of 0 turning the loop into an infinite one - the guard is protecting the algorithm, not just the caller. `slice` clamps past the end on its own, so the ragged final group needs no special case.

sections.title: A Request Is Data Before It Is Traffic
sections.body:
A request is **a value** long before it is traffic: a method, a URL, a set of headers and a body, all of them ordinary JavaScript data. Building that value in one small function puts the interesting decisions - which header carries the token, what the default method is, how a base URL and a path join without doubling the slash - somewhere you can call a thousand times without a server.

Authentication is one of those decisions. A bearer token travels in the `Authorization` header as the literal text `Bearer ` followed by the token, and a client with no token must leave the header out entirely rather than send `Bearer undefined` and collect a 401 it cannot explain.

- A header that does not apply is an **absent key**, never an empty one.
- Headers are a plain object, so adding one is an assignment.

annotations.text: Accept is unconditional - it is what the client always wants back, regardless of who is asking.
An empty-string token is the case that catches people: it is falsy, but it is still a string, and `Bearer ` with nothing after it is worse than no header at all.
Content-Type describes the body you are sending. No body, no header - a GET that announces a JSON body is lying.
Strip every trailing slash from the base, then guarantee exactly one at the front of the path.
Both sides bring a slash here and neither brings one on the next line; both must produce the same URL.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `authHeaders(token)` returning the request headers object. It always carries `Accept: "application/json"`, and it carries `Authorization: "Bearer " + token` **only** when `token` is a non-empty string.
checkpoint.explain: An absent header and an empty one are different requests on the wire. `Authorization: Bearer ` with nothing after it is a credential the server must reject, while no header at all is an anonymous request it can answer or refuse cleanly - so the guard has to rule out the empty string, not just `null`.

sections.title: Reading What Came Back
sections.body:
What comes back is a number and some text, and neither is trustworthy alone. **The status code decides the shape**: 2xx means the body is your data, 4xx means you asked wrongly, 5xx means the server broke at something that was not your fault.

`JSON.parse` throws on anything that is not JSON, and a failing proxy answers with an HTML error page, which is exactly that - so the parse belongs inside a `try`. A 204 carries no body at all, so parsing must be skipped rather than attempted on an empty string.

Normalising both outcomes into one of two shapes - `{ ok, status, data }` or `{ ok, status, error }` - means every caller writes a single `if` instead of a switch over status codes it will get wrong.

annotations.text: A 204 has no body. Guarding here is cheaper than discovering that JSON.parse("") throws.
The parse is the only line that can throw, so it is the only line inside the try.
A well-behaved API explains itself in the body; when it does not, the status code is the only message there is.
A gateway failure is where this pays off - HTML in, a described error out, and no SyntaxError escaping into the caller.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: `JSON.parse` is a parser, not a converter: it happily returns a bare number, and it throws on the empty string rather than handing back `null`. The last line is the one that shapes your API - `JSON.stringify` drops keys whose value is `undefined`, so a result that sets `error: undefined` on success does not carry an empty error field, it carries no such field at all.

sections.title: Retry Only What Might Succeed, and Not Forever
sections.body:
A retry is worth making only when the failure might not repeat. A 500 or a 503 is the server admitting it fell over, and a 429 is it asking you to slow down - both deserve another try. A 404 or a 401 will fail identically forever, so retrying them only multiplies the user's wait.

Two things stop a retry loop from becoming an attack on your own server: a **cap** on the number of attempts, and a **growing wait** between them. Doubling that wait - 100ms, then 200ms, then 400ms - is called **exponential backoff**, and capping it stops the curve from turning a retry into a nap.

annotations.text: 429 is the odd one out: a 4xx that is your fault and still worth retrying, because the server told you to wait rather than to stop.
Math.min is the cap. Without it the eighth retry waits 12.8 seconds and the user has already left.
Attempt numbers are 1-based, so the first wait is the base delay itself.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `attemptDelays(attempts)` returning the array of waits **between** that many tries, in milliseconds: 100 doubling each time, capped at 800. `attemptDelays(3)` is `[100, 200]` and `attemptDelays(1)` is `[]`.
checkpoint.explain: The waits sit between the tries, not after them, so n attempts need n-1 delays and a single attempt needs none - that off-by-one is the difference between a client that returns and one that sleeps on its way out. The cap is what turns an exponential curve into a schedule you could defend to a user watching a spinner.

sections.title: The Transport Is a Parameter
sections.body:
A client's one unavoidable side effect is the network call, so make it **a parameter**. `runRequest(transport, config)` never mentions `fetch`; it calls whatever function it was handed. Production hands it one built on `fetch`, and a test hands it one that returns `{ status: 503 }` on demand.

That is not a workaround for this sandbox, though the sandbox makes it unmissable - there is no network here at all. It is how a retry policy gets tested: no real server will produce two 503s and then a 200 for you, in a millisecond, identically every time. The real runner writes `await transport(request)`, and because `await` hands a plain value straight back, that one line drives a transport that answers at once and one that answers with a promise.

The same discipline applies to waiting. A runner that truly slept 700ms would make its own suite slow and its schedule invisible, so this one **returns the delays it would have waited** and lets the caller decide what to do with them.

annotations.text: The runner does not know what a transport is. It knows only that calling it gives back a response.
A fake transport is two lines. A real server that answers 200 on cue is a machine, a deploy and a bad afternoon.
And this is the one you could never arrange on purpose - a server that is reliably, repeatably down.
Same runner, same request, opposite outcome. Nothing inside the runner changed between the two calls.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `async function tryTwice(transport)`. Call `transport()` and `await` the result. If its `status` is 500 or above, call the transport once more and return that second `status`; otherwise return the first. The transport may answer with a plain object or with a promise.
